items.sum: "Observer" complains that the club does not press to stage county events at St. John's Hall, previews "A" team fixtures and the South of the Thames Junior, answers a letter from Stoke, and gives short biographies of A Robertshaw, J. A. Jones and G. H Powell.
items.s: SPORTS JOTTINGS "Observer" complains that the club does not press to stage county events at St. John's Hall, previews "A" team fixtures and the South of the Thames Junior, answers a letter from Stoke, and gives short biographies of A Robertshaw, J. A. Jones and G. H Powell. I notice that at the monthly committee meeting of the Surrey County A.A.A., Caterham A.C. reported that they were unable to hold the County Junior C.C. race from their headquarters owing to lack of dressing accommodation. It was decided to approach the Ranelagh Harriers with a view to running this race from their headquarters on December 1st Might I ask what about St. John's Hall? Here there is ample dressing accommodation, as witness our Open Walk in which there is over a hundred competitiors; in fact, I make bold to say that I consider our heaquarters to be superior to those of any Club around London. Surely we have on the Surrey Committee someone who could press the claims of our Club to stage this race. Other Clubs have their share of races, the South of Thames Junior, for instance, seems to have become one of Surrey A.C.'s own fixtures. This race was held over Wimbledon Common in 1925, not from our headquarters, but from a hall near where Ashcombe's course commences. True it ended in chaos owing to various reasons, Footer included, that being however another story. My point is that our own Club could stage and house an event of this description and also see it carried through satisfactorily. We have men on these various committees who should advance our claims, but apparently they are not interested. This fact was also noticable during the track season; even the Javelin Championship, with one of our members the most prominent performer in the country, was allocated to a minor Club, and so we could go on down the list. What does it mean? That our officials shirk the responsibility of staging these events, or that they are just not interested? It certainly seems a pity that while a Club like Mitcham A.C. is always willing to help, the Belgrave Harriers remain coldly aloof. I understand that this season's Cross Country fixture list will include a few matches for our "A" team men. The latter are those who are unable to secure a place in the teams for the bigger races, and also our Junior members who should gain useful experience from the contests arranged. If those who are eligible will get together with the promising newcomers and train steadily during the early part of the season, the nucleus of a fine team should be formed for the South of the Thames Junior. We won this event in 1925 and were placed last year, so it's up to our boys to see that they pull it off this time, and so gladden our President's heart. On one point I am sure: that it will not be for want of trying. I see that in our genial friend's letter from Stoke, with its several little home truths, that he considers I am a lady! Perish the thought. I should hate to be considered " one of those." He also mentions vicious remarks. I certainly most humbly beg anyone's pardon if such should have been considered the case I simply state a few facts in a language I am sure you all understand, Paul Khlopin excepted; although I think he is rapidly becoming quite proficient, judging by his "Aw Hell." If there is, of course, anyone who disapproves of what I say, then he has ample room in which to express himself, by sending a letter to the Editor who, I am sure, will give it prominence in our recently opened Correspondence pages. Now that the Summer is over (for information as to when this season occurred I should advise your writing, say, John Bull, as some of my friends are still awaiting this so-called Summer), or to put it better, now that the dark evenings are here and you are, owing to climatic conditions, confined indoors, perhaps the following short biographies will make interesting reading :— A Robertshaw, another of the Club's heroes over the country, ran exceptionally well last season, which incidentally was his first, as prior to this he had competed with success on the cycling track. He settled down to the running game at once, having a steady stride and stamina in abundance, due no doubt to his riding in 25's. Was first man home for the Club in the South of Thames Senior, and I hope to see him lead the whole field home in this year's race. J. A. Jones, one of our recent newcomers from Kensington, is a most versatile runner. Shines especially over the half and has competed with great success at distances from 220yds. up to 5 miles! Has a fine easy motion, and a remarkable turn of speed at the finish of a race. Runs well over the country and will be a strong contender for a place in the Brighton Relay team. G. H Powell, the Club's field event champion; I use this word advisedly, for although the Club has not as yet held any Championships for field events, I am sure they will do so in the future. Owing to the interest which George has aroused among them, several members have, I understand, purchased their own javelins, and are under his able tuition becoming quite proficient at the sport. George, who is the Surrey County, and ex-Southern Counties champion, at the recent Ponders End Sports threw a distance of 183ft. 1in, which is a British Native record. items.label: October 1928
items.sum: Report of the opening of the winter season at St. John's Hall, Wimbledon, on September 29th, with 57 runners and 25 walkers, two training packs, tea and a dance over 100 strong.
items.s: A GOOD START. Report of the opening of the winter season at St. John's Hall, Wimbledon, on September 29th, with 57 runners and 25 walkers, two training packs, tea and a dance over 100 strong. A typical autumn day favoured the opening of our winter season on Saturday, September 29th, at Wimbledon. On arrival at St. John's Hall, we were cheered by the discovery of re-decorations and alterations which will add to our comfort during the next few months. More pleasing still was the large attendance of old and new members, all eager to start the season with early training. It will greatly help the Club if such enthusiasm endures during the less inviting months to come, as that is the proof of a cross-country runner. The actual numbers of active members were 57 runners and 25 walkers. Several others were present who were obviously past it, either through Anno Domini or Avoirdupois, though some of the active seemed to suffer from the latter complaint. Two packs were formed. The fast pack, ably led by our new captain, W. G. Webb, covered five miles at a steady pace, while the slower pack, under W. Rice, ran about 3½ miles. I say ran, but I saw a few who seemed to qualify for our other section. Still, gently does it. After training, a merry party of 65, including many of the fairer sex, enjoyed a good tea, and in fairness to the caterers I must say that they did not supply subject for chaff at the table. After tea and a little rest to let it settle, dancing was commenced and, with constantly increasing numbers, we finished up a good afternoon and evening, over 100 strong. Especially pleasing to us is the increasing number of ladies supporting our socials, and it is incumbent upon a number of our members to learn dancing and provide more partners, or we shall soon be outnumbered. After such a good start, we hope to continue these happy, homely affairs more often than during last season. A.E M. W. G. Webb W. G. Webb new captain; led the fast pack over five miles at the season's opening W. Rice W. Rice led the slower pack about 3½ miles at the season's opening A.E.M. A.E M. initials signing the report A.E M. items.label: October 1928
items.sum: First instalment of P.N.K.'s true story of being thrown on his own resources at 14 in Russia in 1918: trench digging at Beresniki for the Whites and bartering cigarettes for food and a fur coat; to be continued.
items.s: LIFE! (A True Story). First instalment of P.N.K.'s true story of being thrown on his own resources at 14 in Russia in 1918: trench digging at Beresniki for the Whites and bartering cigarettes for food and a fur coat; to be continued. Autumn in 1918! Not one of your English autumns, with rain and fog, but a real Russian full-blooded affair, with snow and frost setting up new records daily. Feeling rather footsore and hungry, I plodded on the 30 mile trail between Konetzgorje and Beresniki, hoping to either enlist the White Russian forces or to find some sort of work. For, owing to the Revolution and subsequent civil war, I was thrown on my own resources at the age of 14, some 1,300 miles from my father's place. Of resources I had a few worthless roubles in my pocket, some slight knowledge derived from a few years' study in a seminary, and plenty of optimism. I got to Beresniki at about 8 in the evening. It was a dark town or rather large village, full of strange talk and stranger oaths. Parties of workmen going home, soldiers, sledges and smoke from thousands of chimneys. Rather awed by the babel of voices in the main street, I turned off, selected a kind looking house, and knocked at the door. The housewife came out. Now to her, in this issue of the Belgravian, want to make a full apology. For to her I told a tale of fearful woe, lying shamelessly, as only a student can ..... Sick father, mother with a horde of hungry children (I forget how many I said), myself the eldest (this part was true) and the only bread-winner. "My poor boy," she cried, "come right in and warm yourself." In I went into a large typically Russian room, lit by a hanging paraffin lamp. Round the table sat a party of workmen who lodged there, having tea. My tale evoked general sympathy and I was bid to have a meal. Of this I was sadly in need, as I had walked all that day on only a few scones. I was questioned about my intentions and laughed at when I talked about "joining up." "You are far too small," said my landlord "Now, I know the foreman in charge of trench digging and I will try and get you a job." After supper I was put to sleep on a lot of straw in a row with some dozen workmen. Few times since have I slept better! True to his promise the good man took me to the foreman, to whom I told my story, in which by this time I began to believe not a little bit myself. Touched to the roots of his beard, this despot told me to report to work next morning, giving me a letter to the warehouse. In this place I was given a pick and a shovel, together with a threat of retribution to follow should I lose them. Next morning I turned out. Trench digging! Those of you who are old enough think of France and Belgium and mud. Not so here. Roughly, the procedure was this. First we had to burn a huge log fire along the proposed line of the trench. After a few hours of this we had to dig like the devil, lest the ground froze harder than ever! The idea was to build a chain of small fortresses along the river bank, to check the supposed Bolshevik advance in the spring, after the ice-break. This never came, but we worked on. Lord, how I used to work those days! Throwing clay well above my head was bad enough, but the real tit-bit was sand-bag filling. These we had to carry along a plank to the walls of the blockhouse. Now, I suppose I wasn't very strong for a lad of 14, as for the life of me I could not lift a filled bag to my shoulder. So I evolved an original plan. Grasping the bag around the middle, I used to carry it along like a load of hay—pressed to my stomach! However, real fun began after knocking off. Food was scarce those days and I had to forage for myself. Owing to cheapness of Russian roubles, cigarettes used to be the coin of exchange, besides the time-honoured bartering system. For cigarettes, and of these I used to hoard a large store, got by fair and foul means, I used to buy my food. From mess cooks whose integrity I fear was not above reproach, I used to get tins of bully-beef, maconochie, biscuits, etc. Though of food I had plenty, I used nearly to freeze to death working in my thin college clothes, with the temperature at zero. Now, at my lodging house, lived a youngster of about 18, on whose fine fur coat I cast many an envious glance. One evening, during my bartering expedition, for 100 cigarettes or so, I got a pair of army boots and puttees. Now, these were apparently of no earthly use to me, but I had my ideas. Home I went, my trophies slung carelessly over my shoulder. Christmas was near. My fur-coated friend wanted to go home for the holidays. But going home he meant to look a swell. About the latter he had rather original ideas, for army boots and puttees were his acme of smartness. Of this I took rather unfair advantage, for although he was 18, mentally he was no match for me. The end of it was that he went off home in new boots, leaving his coat with me! I sincerely hope he got home all right, for 40 miles of snow trail in army boots and scanty clothes is no joke, even for a grown-up. But I meant to be warm. P.N.K. (To be continued, subject to the Editor's permission and your patience) P.N.K. P.N.K. Konetzgorje Beresniki Russia France Belgium

items.label: October 1928
items.sum: A new contributor writing as "Half-Circle" introduces a column of verses, anecdotes and jokes: a verse in praise of a Belgrave cross-country run, then running jokes including George Cummings the professional walker mistaken for a ghost.
items.s: RANDOM REMARKS. A new contributor writing as "Half-Circle" introduces a column of verses, anecdotes and jokes: a verse in praise of a Belgrave cross-country run, then running jokes including George Cummings the professional walker mistaken for a ghost. "Can we not add to our staff of journalists? is a question asked in our last issue. Just sleep on it. I did, and the vanity which crept into my ambitious soul set the pulses throbbing. I slept again. "Who would not be a real live journalist and (oh, dreamy heights!) a contributor to that mighty organ of the press, the Belgravian?" Hysterics disturbed my slumber! I have never written anything— at least anything that the whole world can read if it cares. So must I, on that account, inform our Editor that as far as I am concerned, he is unlucky? No! Here is an opportunity, possibly the only opportunity of a life-time, to enter the realms of the pen. True, no remuneration is given, but none is asked, and how can monetary reward compare with the honour of writing for the journal of journals? And yet I pause in this intention, my courage faints, and in a little voice I plead; forgive me if my efforts do not bear professional stamp; be kind if my construction is sometimes shaky, and always bear with a novice who wishes to add to the success of "our Mag." It is best for you and me, reader, that I make my début under a nom-de-plume I purpose my best with verses, anecdotes, jokes and "things we should like to know;" may our Mag. live through the ordeal. I have recollection of a relative of mine who was a big man on the Star. I believe it was outside Victoria Station that he had his pitch. I did hear that he afterwards became a free-lance—Star, News or Standard. With such talent in the family I may take heart. (With acknowledgment to A. D. Pyer, who, I believe, introduced verse into the Mag.). To novices and those who have never tried a cross-country run; to cotton-wool sprinters, half-milers and the like; to cold catching football-spectating club-members; and to fire-hugging winter book-worms, I dedicate these few lines. I tell you, lad, there is no fun Like a jolly steady cross-country run, For we travel o'er fields and heath so green, Fairer than any you have seen. The air is keen, but pure as gold; Your'e fit and strong as a Spartan of old; Troubles flee when away, my lad, you go, Pleasant life—when you feel aglow. Steady's the gait, no "killing" pace, No one left behind—not a hopeless chase, But a sporting run in the care-free air, Who's the sportsman would not be there? A bath comes after, steaming hot, Bread and butter, cakes, and tea from the pot, Washed and dressed, you will be another man, Sorry for him who never ran. Put down that book; come, leave the fire, London's country calls, and bids you acquire Taste for beautiful scenes and wholesome fun— The pleasures of a Belgrave run. It is on record that a prisoner who escaped from Wandsworth Prison deceived several policemen on point duty by running along in his undervest and short pants. He was, consequently, mistaken for a runner, but this does not infer that runners look like convicts George Cummings, the professional walker, whilst in a certain locality, was obliged to do his training after dusk, owing to the stifling heat at that particular time of the year. On approaching the outskirts of the village during one of his usual spins, he was fired upon by a farmer with a double-barrelled gun. Later enquiries proved that he had been mistaken for a ghost, since he was dressed in white and passed the spot regularly, night after night. No harm was done, however, as the fear-striken man closed his eyes when taking aim. "Hullo! old man, training for a race?" "No idiot, racing for a train." The champion local sprinter was challenged to a fifty yards dash by a young builder's labourer, provided the latter should name his own course. The champion accepted and asked where the course might be He was shown a ladder. Mrs. Smith was congratulating Mrs. Brown on her son's good performances at the local sports "They did say he simply burnt up the track," said Mrs. Smith. "So I believe, as I had a look at the sports ground to-day and did see nothing but cinders," replied Mrs. Brown, the dear old soul. I feel obliged to tell this one, since it was concocted by a very popular Club official. "Hullo! George old chap, how are things progressing?" "Oh, not too bad. I'm a manager now" "Really?" "Yes! I just manage to get to work at eight o'clock each morning." THINGS WE SHOULD LIKE TO KNOW— If a certain Club member of road-running fame intends to take up dirt-track racing, as he has just acquired a second-hand machine, presumably for practice. Does he consider running with the beast in an effort to start it to be good training? What is a "Footer Finish?" Why a sack race specialist failed to obtain a prize in this class of event this year Possibly he found the sacks a little too large this time. Who is "Observer?" Why a certain Club official fails to return borrowed boxes of matches. No criminal intent, I feel sure. A. D. Pyer A. D. Pyer credited with introducing verse into the Belgravian George Cummings George Cummings professional walker; anecdote of being shot at while training after dusk in white Victoria Station Wandsworth Prison

items.label: October 1928
items.sum: Letter from V. J. Peacock criticising the two-hour election of officers at the Annual General Meeting and proposing advance nominations with circulated ballot papers and postal votes.
items.s: CORRESPONDENCE. Letter from V. J. Peacock criticising the two-hour election of officers at the Annual General Meeting and proposing advance nominations with circulated ballot papers and postal votes. To the Editor. Dear Sir, There is one aspect of our Annual General Meeting to which I would like to call particular attention, while it is still fresh in the memory. This is in connection with the election of officers. It will be generally agreed, I am convinced, that almost two hours were taken up by these elections. Moreover, many names were submitted without mature consideration and some names were put forward facetiously. When our worthy President asked "Any more nominations?" someone or other usually thought of a name, doubled it, took away the name he first thought of, and proposed it! (Except of course when it happened to be for the election of the President, or the Hon. Secretary, or the Hon Treasurer. There could be no two minds as to who should fill these parts). Various people bobbed up and down to get behind screens while their fates were being decided Two paper ballots were made and many of the names in the lists were unknown to a large portion of the meeting. It is vitally important for any organisation that its officers should be elected with care, and I suggest that our rules be amended to allow the inclusion of the following method of voting. At a date not less than four weeks prior to the Annual General Meeting, each member should be notified as to the date and place of the meeting. This notification should be accompanied by a list of those officers who seek re-election, and further nominations to any office should be invited. These further nominations should be in the Secretary's hands not less than fourteen days before the date of the meeting. Ballot papers would then be prepared and circulated, together with the agenda for the meeting. The ballot papers when completed, could either be brought personally to the Meeting or (if the individual cannot be present in person) sent by post to the Secretary, prior to the meeting. All votes would then be counted at the meeting. Besides the two hours of time saved at the meeting itself, each individual would have time to make any enquiries concerning the people for whom he is voting. This method of election has worked very smoothly for many years in another Club to which I belong, and I would be glad if you would open your columns to comments on the proposal. I prefer to get other opinions before putting down a definite resolution for the next A.G.M. I am, Sir, Yours sincerely, V. J. Peacock. V. J. Peacock V. J. PEACOCK. letter proposing advance nominations and postal ballot for election of officers

items.label: October 1928
items.sum: Letter to the Editor speculating on the identity of the anonymous contributor "Observer" and suggesting it is Harry Parker.
items.s: Letter to the Editor speculating on the identity of the anonymous contributor "Observer" and suggesting it is Harry Parker. To the Editor. Dear Sir, In common with many other readers of The Belgravian, I have read with interest and appreciation the notes contributed by "Observer," and become more and more intrigued each month as to the identity of this mysterious writer who prefers to remain anonymous. Is he old or young? Dark or fair? Runner or walker? Or is "Observer" a lady as suggested by Ken O'Kell in his breezy letter from Stoke? From his authoritative writings is is evident that he is well informed and a member of the Committee. The fact that in his short biographies he has not, up to the present, included any walkers suggests that he is (or has been) a runner. Lastly, it is unlikely that anyone would give his own biography, and so it is useless to look among the names that have already appeared for this modern "Junius." In conclusion I would suggest that "Observer" is Harry Parker, and await his denial and any remarks other readers may care to make on this subject through the columns of The Belgravian. Yours, etc., H. H. H. Ken O'Kell Ken O'Kell had suggested in a letter from Stoke that "Observer" is a lady Harry Parker Harry Parker suggested by the writer as the anonymous contributor "Observer" Stoke

e: South of the Thames Junior Championship
items.s: CLUB NOTES Club notes on the Berman Cup and South of the Thames Junior wins, two proposed inter-club summer competitions, and new members and resignations. Honours fall thick upon us. To have won the "Berman" Cup and the South of the Thames Junior Championship, when we can be no more than getting into our stride, must satisfy the most ambitious of our enthusiasts. Yet, while we are justifiably puffed with pride, we must look ahead to the big races of the new year and conserve our energies for still greater triumphs. Already our Committee are at work on the programme for next summer season. Two projects which have received favourable comment in the Committee-room are outlined here. The first is that we should take part in a four-cornered relay and team match of 4 events (4 x 100yds , 4 x 440yds., 1 mile team race and 2 miles walk, team race) with Highgate H., Sambridge H. and Herne Hill H at Finsbury Park. The match would be decided by points, on the same lines as the "Doris" and "Inter-Club Relay" Shields competitions, which have always been so popular with us. The second suggestion, from the S L.H , concerns Achilles Club, Herne Hill H., London A.C., Surrey A C. and the Polytechnic H., besides themselves and our own Club. It is for the formation of an athletic league in which each club will meet the others in turn, once during the season, in a team match. The events would be as in the former suggestion, but without the walk, and in addition 4 x 220yds., 4 x 880yds. and 4 x 120yds. hurdles (shuttle), relays. Field events (high jump, long jump, putting the shot and throwing the javelin) would be included, too. What a galaxy of athletic opportunity ! items.label: November 1928
items.h: INTER-CLUB C.C. RACE WITH ASHCOMBE A.C AND THAMES VALLEY A.C. (5 MILES).
items.sum: Report and result of the 5-mile inter-club cross-country race at Feltham on 20 October with Ashcombe A.C. and Thames Valley A.C., won by Belgrave with 77 points.
e: Inter-Club C.C. Race with Ashcombe A.C. and Thames Valley A.C.
items.s: INTER-CLUB C.C. RACE WITH ASHCOMBE A.C AND THAMES VALLEY A.C. (5 MILES). Report and result of the 5-mile inter-club cross-country race at Feltham on 20 October with Ashcombe A.C. and Thames Valley A.C., won by Belgrave with 77 points. Apparently a cross-country race is an exciting affair to watch. At least, that is what I and a small band of supporters thought on Saturday, October 20th, when more than thirty Belgravians went down to Feltham to compete in their first race over the country this season. As usual, we were much too strong for the other two clubs, who had a keen race, however, for second place in the team contest; Ashcombe beating the Valley by only one point. Khlopin, as we expected was leading round the rather dangerous bend some hundred yards from the start, but he was soon passed by Cohen and Pyer. We were surprised to see how the field had spread out after half a mile. Cohen had set up a very fast pace, but he was soon caught and passed by Bicknell. Pyer was third, some distance behind, but well ahead of the rest of the field. This order for the leaders remained the same to the end. At half-way it was very strange to see Footer as far back as the thirties—he was taking a friend along—but it was not strange, but merely wonderful, to see him tearing in at the finish—ninth ! Many remarks were made in regard to Footer's method of dealing with obstacles. Ordinary people either climb over or crawl underneath, but he seems to dive through without breaking his stride and without so much as a "Pardon" to the slighted obstacle Another spectacular feature was the easy running of Duffett and W. G. Webb, who appeared to be jogging round having a yarn and yet finished fifth and sixth respectively. The average runner has to "run his eyeballs out" to get into the twenties, yet our two running captains can get up to the leaders by means of a little gentle trotting. It has already been mentioned that Bicknell was first man home. He finished unchallenged at quite a fast pace and in perfect style, looking as though he had enjoyed running over his own course. Mickey Pyer was first man to score for the Belgrave and was still well ahead of the bunch which included those two captains who scorn racing. The latter were looking round to count up the fact that we had ten in thirteen, and it is understood that they were very relieved to discover that there was no need for them to start hurrying after all. A figure in white was seen to dart from the above-mentioned bunch and run into fourth place and become second man to score for us. This was A. Penny, who had run remarkably well. Penny is a useful miler on the track and was third in our opening race on the road at Wimbledon. It is safe to prophesy that he will be another strong addition to our team. Robertshaw, perhaps our most successful runner last winter, was only nineteenth. He is not yet fit, which is all to the good, for he is not likely to become stale at the time of our more important races next February and March. Of the others who finished well up, mention should be made of S R Chorley, who is "streets" better than he was last year, and our former walking secretary, in his first cross-country race for two years, did well to finish thirteenth with plenty in hand. Throughout he had been running comfortably and he makes running look a very easy sort of business Most of the others, apart from the leaders, looked the worse for wear In conclusion (and by way of a digression) I would like to give a tip to officials. It is their duty to be dignified and to earn respect from all I will therefore tell them that the man with an umbrella who witnessed this contest was addressed as "Sir" by one of the competitors L.E F. e: Inter-Club Race (Thames Valley Harriers and Ashcombe A.C.)
items.s: INTER-CLUB RACE. Report and results of the second inter-club cross-country race with Thames Valley and Ashcombe at Wimbledon on 10 November, run with the Club 5 miles Sealed Handicap; Belgrave won with 256 points. At Wimbledon, on November 10th. Club 5 miles Sealed Handicap in conjunction. Our Club's numerical strength was again demonstrated in the second Inter-Club Race with T V H and A.A.C., as although both the opposing clubs had more starters than at the first meeting, we again mustered more than they could field together. In fact there were just 100 starters and I think 60 were Belgravians The large field made for more to score, and 18 a side was decided upon. Of course, this was very much in our favour, and our 18 were actually in the first 26 places. Probably the Club Sealed Handicap, incorporated in the race, was an incentive to our chaps, and produced a very close field. Even closer were the placings in the Handicap The short space of 26 seconds separated the first 10 men. The race itself was very interesting, as there was the prospect of a fine tussle for individual honours. After a fast start, Allum (Belgrave) led at the first turn, with Cohen (Ashcombe) close behind Getting on to the golf links, Cohen took over the lead, but hereabouts Footer came through with a rush and, using Sandy Hill to the best advantage, went to the front. The order through the Brook was Footer, Cohen, Flower, Junr., Duffett, Pyer, Rice and Allum Then came a minor tragedy as Footer suddenly decided to go round the rough field instead of across it, thereby losing the lead and about 70 or 80 yards of ground, which, of course, he could not make up on Cohen, although he passed the rest of us again. Going up the Horse-Ride, Bicknell (T.V.H.) and Penny (Belgrave) put in some good running and got into the first 6 places. Except for a new T.V.H. member in Porter, who made a good effort across the common home, the other positions remained unaltered For the rest, A. G. Jones ran very well, as we thought he was short of training, and S Chorley again got home in the first 25. In fact, the whole of the South of Thames Junior A Team showed up well. S. Drake has certainly improved in winning this very close handicap The "Footer" school had a good day, as R. Freestone took the Novice's Prize, and H. E. himself took 2 awards. Coleman, on his running, merits watching in the Surrey County Junior Race. W.A.R. RESULTS * Dead Heat † Winner of Novice Prize. Belgrave H . 2 3 5 6 8 9 10 11 13 16 17 18 20 21 22 24 25 26 — 256 pts. items.sum: Report, Belgrave positions and team placings from the South of the Thames Junior cross-country race at Epsom Downs on 17 November, won by the Belgrave A team with 22 points.
e: South of the Thames Junior Championship
items.s: SOUTH OF THE THAMES JUNIOR. Report, Belgrave positions and team placings from the South of the Thames Junior cross-country race at Epsom Downs on 17 November, won by the Belgrave A team with 22 points. The South of the Thames Junior Race, Surrey and Berks, took place in splendid weather at Epsom Downs, on November 17th. Our Club had 4 teams entered, a record, I believe, for this race, and although some of the selected men failed to turn up, we managed to start the 4 teams. What is more, they all closed-in, a very satisfactory display There was a large field of runners, and at the fall of the flag our boys were well away. Wesson, of Epsom, forced the pace at the start, with Allum of our own Club lying 2nd The rest of our "A" team were close behind. At a mile W. S. Mitchell, Belgrave H , had taken the lead, followed by L. J. Cohen, of Ashcombe. Allum, Rice and Penny were close on their heels. In fact, our 4 were in the first 6. Hopes beat high in our breasts, and we were not disappointed. For when the field came in sight once more, Mitchell, although deposed from the lead by Cohen, was running finely, and our other men, Penny and Allum, were having a battle royal for 3rd place Three in four ! It was all over, for Rice, although dropping several places, came along in the 13th position and we had won an easy and handsome victory It was a case of " well run all !" a very fine performance and one that justified our high hopes of those three most promising members, namely, W. S. Mitchell, A. W. Penney and A. Allum. I only hope that Mrs. Allum, who was one of the many supporters present at the race, was as pleased as we were. The remaining 4 of our "A" team ran well together, and fully justified their selection. Although it hardly seems fair to mention individuals, everyone having run so well, a word of praise is due to F. G. Ford who ran, although feeling far from well, and also to C. R. Strange, H W. Swetman, R. Hickey and R. Freestone, who all ran extremely well, and should, if they persevere, improve on their performances. items.sum: Running secretary's review of December fixtures: Surrey Youths' Race team, a social run at Mitcham, the third inter-club race, the Club 7 Miles Championship and the Boxing Day meeting.
e: Inter-Club Race (Thames Valley Harriers and Ashcombe A.C.)
items.s: RUNNING Running secretary's review of December fixtures: Surrey Youths' Race team, a social run at Mitcham, the third inter-club race, the Club 7 Miles Championship and the Boxing Day meeting. We have some attractive fixtures during the next month and perhaps a brief review of them might be helpful to a few members. On December 1st the following team will compete in the Surrey Youths' Race, to be held from the headquarters of the Ranelagh H., viz., J. G. Coleman, A. C. Canard, S. Garland, T. C. Jones, D. Mann, L. C. Clapham, A. L Sanders and A. A. G. Thorne. The response of our junior members in support of this race is disappointing, but we hope for better support next year. On December 8th we have a big day. Social Run with our old friends, Croydon H., Epsom H. and Mitcham A.C., from the headquarters of the latter at Rose Hill Farm, Sutton, followed by a social evening at the White Hart Hotel, Mitcham All runners and friends are asked to come along and swell the merry throng. On the same day a team will be representing our Club in a race versus St. George's Services from their abode at Mitcham; team will be selected and notified as usual These runners will rejoin the main body at the White Hart in the evening. The third inter-club race between Ashcombe, T.V.H. and ourselves will be held on December 15th, from the former's headquarters at Roehampton. It is hoped that our boys will support this fixture as well as they have done the previous ones, and so keep up our record attendances. December 22nd is the date of the Club's 7 Miles Championship for the Blackstaffe Shield (Holder, A. Clark) A new course of 2 laps has been selected, and in conjunction with the race will be a Sealed Handicap, which I trust all members will support, as although some consider themselves out of it, so far as Championship placings are concerned, I should like to remind them of the Handicap. I am sure that, given a fine entry, our Handicapper will be in a most lenient mood. " Boxing Day," our own Powderhall meeting, the one the sharp brigade wait for Here it is : handicaps to suit all, for sprinters a 120yds race, for the distance men a 2 miles run. Now then, boys, here is your chance to take home, not a turkey, but one of the many handsome prizes that are to be given. Bring your friends along, they won't go to bed the previous night, so get them to make a 24 hour shift of it by coming to Battersea Park to see you run. E. A. DUFFETT, Hon Running Sec. J. G. items.s: R W.A. 7 MILES WALK. Report and result of the R.W.A. 7 miles walk at Bowes Park on 27 October, in which Belgrave won the Berman Cup for the winning team. A record field of 231 individuals and 28 teams started at Bowes Park on October 27th. We were successful in securing the "Berman" Cup, presented to the winning team in the level race, from the holders, Surrey A C. J. G. Scamell was again very speedy and led our team home F. H. Elson, who was next, was only a few yards in front of R. D McMullen, with whom he had walked all the way, and J. E. Field provided our fourth. As F. Rickards followed Field in, we were pretty safe for a fourth man. Such a capture as the "Berman" Cup is a worthy sequel to the fine record of last season. Both E. Saunders and W. G. Dodkin walked better than ever before, and the former gained third place in the handicap J. J. Cricton, in his first open road walk, showed considerable promise. We were the only Club to enter three teams for the race, and the walking of our "juniors" (in the road-walking sense) could hardly have been better. Altogether it was an auspicious start. RESULT. items.label: November 1928
items.sum: Walking secretary's notes on December fixtures: the Croydon–Banstead and back race with Surrey W.C., a match against the Metropolitan Police, the Horwood Cup junior race and the Boxing Day Godstone walk.
items.s: WALKING. Walking secretary's notes on December fixtures: the Croydon–Banstead and back race with Surrey W.C., a match against the Metropolitan Police, the Horwood Cup junior race and the Boxing Day Godstone walk. December will be a busy month for walkers. On the 1st we shall be engaged in the annual Croydon—Banstead and back race with the Surrey W.C. (11¾ miles). Last year we were the losers through a weak tail, although we had the first two men to finish. This time we hope to remedy the defect. McMullen, Dodkin, Cricton, Carne and Rathbone have already promised to be there, and they, with Green Rickards, and Manning, will make a redoubtable team. On the following Saturday we meet the Metropolitan Police. All our resources must be summoned to beat this "touring side," but again I am sure we can rely on our boys. The first Belgrave man will, as usual, receive a small prize. The date for the "Horwood Cup" (Junior) race is December 15th. The event is eagerly awaited and promises to be one of the most exciting "tear-ups" of the year. It will be worth watching. A handicap is held in conjunction, so that the splendid pack of novices which we have coming-on, may share in the spoils. Quite a number of our men have "Godstone" ambitions, and are using the "Banstead" as training to this end. The race, of course, takes place on Boxing Day ("weather permitting" we should add, smilingly, with memories of last Boxing Day) and the distance is about 18¾ miles. The course is a difficult one. Walkers of tender years will find the Three Miles Handicap at Battersea Park more suited to their capabilities. B J T KNIFTON, Hon Walking Sec. The most promising members at this sport are Hegarty, Fleming, Noble, White, Pyer and Williams (W.H.). Those who started in the summer, and any others, are invited to turn out on Sunday mornings at Battersea Park, so that we may be well represented in the matches which are being arranged to take place, in addition to the usual inter-club track events. We particularly want some hefty fellows as weight-putters, and new members should be introduced, to take up this branch of athletics. G H. POWELL, Capt. Field Events. items.label: November 1928
items.sum: Account of the tea, entertainment and dance after the inter-club run on Wimbledon Common on 10 November 1928.
items.s: SOCIAL HELD AT WIMBLEDON, NOV. 10th, 1928. Account of the tea, entertainment and dance after the inter-club run on Wimbledon Common on 10 November 1928. A very hard run with T.V.H. and A.A.C., in which the "Bels" had a run-away victory, and the wide open spaces of Wimbledon Common, had given everybody an enormous appetite. Afterwards we were joined by members of the London Olympiades and Poly. Ladies—a hundred of us sat down to tea. Judging by the consumption, I feel convinced that all had a good "bob's worth;" surely the tea that is provided by the Bels. cannot be "touched" for quality, quantity and service, anywhere After the tea we were treated to some good entertainment. C. Boud created a fine success with two songs Then that dapper little chap. W. H. Williams, also captured the applause. The talent of these Club members was highly appreciated. Miss Fish, daughter of "Smiling Bill," upheld the ladies' side and gave us a good song. Of course, W. L. Bayliss accompanied the items, as usual—no easy task—and we are indebted to him. On arrival of the dance band, we all had a chance to show our paces. Why the devil do you all sit round the room like wallflowers? For goodness' sake, you great big mothers' darlings, get up and make the girls dance with you! (My sympathy is with the girls). What is the use of a dance band when you all sit and stare? It is entirely up to everyone to make himself sociable. A new member of ours, P. J. E. Cook, did us a great favour by persuading his sister to entertain us (some baby, eh!). After singing us a "love" song, she followed with some fine dancing, Some of our boys, I noticed, bucked-up considerably; they seemed ready for another five miles! W. H. Williams again obliged, and further items from Miss Cook brought the "turns" to a close. I take this opportunity of thanking all who helped in arranging this very successful evening, especially the artists who so willingly came forward. We want additional artists for future occasions. Don't hide your light under a bushel! C. Boud C. Boud sang two songs at the social W. H. Williams W. H. items.label: November 1928
items.h: SOCIAL RUN WITH HIGHATE AND POLY H AT EDGWARE, NOV 3rd, 1928
items.sum: Account of the social run from Edgware with Highgate and Poly. H. on 3 November 1928, with tea and a card-party on the train home.
items.s: SOCIAL RUN WITH HIGHATE AND POLY H AT EDGWARE, NOV 3rd, 1928 Account of the social run from Edgware with Highgate and Poly. H. on 3 November 1928, with tea and a card-party on the train home. The prospects of a fine afternoon, high tea and a social afterwards, and perhaps the recollection of the good time certain members in particular had last year, attracted a large number of our runners to Edgware. Poly. H. had been invited also, so we turned out over a hundred strong. Our walkers were at Wimbledon trying-out the new course for our "open" walk, and strangely enough, the Highgate walkers gave the fixture little support. Eventually slow, medium and fast packs were sent out. Most of the Bels were in the fast pack, which covered about 7 miles The country was not of the best, owing to awkward hedges, fences and unpleasant odours The hold-ups at the obstacles enabled the stragglers to come up, and so the writer was present when the pack ran across the course of the Mary Ward A.C during the latter club's 5 miles handicap. There followed a "tear-up" for a mile or so, in which the back-markers were unofficially paced. There was a notable absence of the usual "tear-in" at the end of the run, no doubt due to the liberal quantity of hot water which was awaiting us. Tea supplies were rather short, but since our Paul was satisfied, "nuff sed." In spit of our expectations, there was no social after tea, so we exchanged good wishes with our hosts and departed. Before the train had left the platform a card-party was in full swing, and Bert Footer's facial expressions when holding four aces and a king, were a tonic for anyone. Another large party listened while H J. Bignall, Highgate's Olympic representative, related his Amsterdam experiences, and it was a jolly gathering which at length broke up. W.A R. items.label: November 1928
items.sum: The new social secretary's appeal for support of the club's socials and dances, including the dance at Wandsworth Town Hall on 30 November 1928.
items.s: SOCIAL SECTION. The new social secretary's appeal for support of the club's socials and dances, including the dance at Wandsworth Town Hall on 30 November 1928. The expression "Social" may not impress some members of our prospering Club It is true that socials, dances, etc, may not actually improve an athlete's ability, but by meeting fellow-members at these functions friendships are formed, which would not have come about in the ordinary way. We wish to encourage a friendly and sociable atmosphere among our members; this will be achieved, I am sure, by everybody's support of our Socials at Wimbledon, and Dances to be held in the course of the season. Get to know one another, and you will find training a still greater pleasure, that constrained feeling of new members in the dressing room will soon vanish. I have arranged a rather full programme for this season; several Socials are included, but don't forget THE DANCE at Wandsworth Town Hall on the 30th of this month. Dances are not usually a financial success, but with the membership we have, they should pay for themselves As the new Hon. Sec. of this section, I am anxious to make a big success of the Club's social side, and look for your hearty support. Suggestions for new social activities likely to find favour in the Club are asked for especially. Don't forget the Dance—November 30th, 1928, at Wandsworth Town Hall. H. L. ROLLINS, Social Hon. Sec. H. L. Rollins H. L. ROLLINS Social Hon. Sec. (new) Wimbledon Wandsworth Town Hall

items.label: November 1928
items.sum: Column by "Observer" on a starting pen for handicap races, a higher subscription for a free Gazette, wearing Club vests, and short biographies of G. Still, W. G. Dodkin and L. Storey.
items.s: SPORTS JOTTINGS Column by "Observer" on a starting pen for handicap races, a higher subscription for a free Gazette, wearing Club vests, and short biographies of G. Still, W. G. Dodkin and L. Storey. In the Club's recent Three Mile Road Race, it was noticed that the system of starting the men off their marks was not satisfactory. There was the inevitable encroaching on to higher marks, with the result that some gained, while the men further back in the handicap had to suffer. I think that next year we should use some patent starting trap, say in the form of a pen into which the men file as their names are called. Talking of traps, here is surely a fine opportunity for some budding inventor to invent a patent starting scheme for sprinters. Picture a trap on similar lines to which the greyhounds use; men on their marks, into the trap, set, then up goes the flap and they are away to a guaranteed level start. Anyone attempting a flier would get a nasty crack on the head, so I don't think you would find many of the flying school in them. Well, here it is, and if anybody wishes to make use of this suggestion to the A.A.A., they are at perfect liberty to do so. The question of collecting money, due from members, for the Gazette is, I understand, causing our worthy Editor no little inconvenience. It is the practice of a very well known walking club to issue a copy of their Gazette free to all its members, a practice which I would like to see operating in our own Club, but then their subscription is 10/6 per annum, whereas ours in only 6/-. So we arrive at this point: would it not be better to increase our subscription and so have a free Gazette? After all, the latter is a necessary part of any athletic club and I think our members will all agree that our own wants some beating in this respect. One point is clear · it costs money to produce this journal, and while members are so slack about paying for their issues, the whole thing is becoming a financial burden to the Club. Therefore my alternative is to raise the annual subscription by 4/- which is the cost of a year's Gazettes to each member. Under the new subscription they would receive their bulletins gratis. The Inter-Club Race at Feltham saw our leading men finishing consecutively from 3rd position down to 10th. Very nice to see, but with one disappointing feature: some of them were not wearing Club vests and so, instead of an unbroken line of claret and gold, one saw the line broken by blue and black, and white vests. I should like to see our members wearing Club vests in all races, whether Inter-Club or Opens, and so bring the good old claret and gold well before the public eye. Vests can be had on application to our genial Treasurer, Albert Macher, and I trust that members will accept this hint in the spirit in which it is given. The question of my identity appears to be causing a few people some sleepless nights. I feel very flattered, I assure you, but really think they could make better use of their writing abilities, for even if my identity is discovered, what useful purpose would it serve? However, if my readers really want a clue, one of Edgar Wallace's own particular brand, here it is :Columbia Record No 4942, and you will know my guilty secret. With the Road Walking season now commenced in earnest, I shall from time to time include some of our heel and toe exponents in my series of short biographies. My next three include, foremost, one of the old brigade of the running world and one who has fought many stirring battles with the stars of the past, including the ex-mile record holder, Joe Binks — G. Still, now in the veteran stage, but still as keen as ever, and moreover still respected by our Handicapper in Club races over the country. George, who is a life member of the Highgate Harriers, had a distinguished career while with the Gatebearers; he was in their winning National teams of 1904 and 1905, finishing 16th and 19th respectively. He has, however, been with us for many years now, and is always willing to help the younger members along, and I am sure that if George could be persuaded to write his reminiscences, they would make very interesting reading. W. G. Dodkin, used to be well-known as a runner, being in the winning team of the Sussex Junior race while a member of Brighton and County H. He has not experienced the best of luck while with our Club, being troubled by illness, and he has now forsaken the running game and has joined the walkers. Shews great promise, and has gained a few awards in his new sphere, he should be successful in Club and Open Handicaps before the season ends. L. Storey, a young member of our walking section, and one who has shewn wonderful improvement under, so I am told, the guidance of that old diehard, Bill Fish. Storey, after finishing second in the Club Novices' Walk, caught the Handicapper napping and credited himself with 2 wins and a 3rd in successive races. He should do well during the winter, although, being rather young, he might with profit to himself, take things steady until next summer; a remark which applies to several of our younger members, both runners and walkers. items.label: November 1928
items.sum: Continued memoir of a youth in Russia in 1918–19, filling sandbags, then wood-splitting for the R.F.C. and joining a Labour Battalion under Corporal Preston.
items.s: LIFE! (A True Story). (Continued) Continued memoir of a youth in Russia in 1918–19, filling sandbags, then wood-splitting for the R.F.C. and joining a Labour Battalion under Corporal Preston. Just before Christmas of 1918 (which I remember very well, on account of the number of empty rum jars scattered in the snow throughout the village) the foreman in charge of sand-bag filling gave us the so-called "piece-job" This meant we had a certain amount of work to do in allotted time; the sooner we finished it, the sooner we went on our holiday. So far, so good; but certain bright spirits devised an original labour-saving plan As you know, the earth for the bags was frozen, but here was snow just as hard and much easier to get. So into our "sand" bags went about 50 per cent of snow, and we finished our 6 days' job in 3½ days—then holidays! In the spring I went to look at these sand walls—just as well the Bolsheviks never came! Christmas over, I optimistically turned out again, only to be told that the blockhouse work was finished and that I must unload sledges. This meant carrying endless loads of provisions and ammunition all day, supervised this time, not by an easy-going Russian foreman, but by armed soldiers. Here, again, I got under the influence of certain labour economists. After turning up in the morning and doing about an hour's work, we used to slip away, get into an empty barge by the river and play cards till about 5 p.m., when we got back and reported attendance! In those days I could teach our train excursionists something about gambling However, this was too good to last, and, sure enough, soon we were told that in future only local labour would be employed. This was the beginning of a very lean time for me, as no work meant no cigarettes, and no cigarettes meant no food. Having nothing to barter, I set out, like Alexander, in search of fresh worlds to explore, if not to conquer About 3 miles away from the village, along the river bank, lay 6 ice-bound barges, on which were quartered men and officers of the R F C. (now the R A.F.) and there I directed my footsteps one morning in January. On the deck of the last barge a thick-set man, with a red face adorned with bristling moustaches, was splitting firewood. There was nothing remarkable in his occupation, but what amazed me was the flow of profanity which accompanied his work, to which obviously he was not used. Taking my courage in both hands, up I went by the steps "What do you want? Be off," he shouted, demonstrating his meaning by an eloquent motion of the boot. And, really, I must have looked particularly Bolshevistic in my ill-gotten fur coat and Russian felt boots. But I was not so easily frightened and, pointing to the pile of wood on the deck, I said in my best English, "Chop 'em. Come on?" "Come on" was a nick-name given by Russian workmen to English soldiers for their endless exhortations. With evident relief, he handed me the pole-axe, and in quite a short time I had finished his wood for him. Pleased, he took me to the kitchen and dished me a huge plateful of oatmeal. Now, at the risk of offending our Social Secretary (who provides our Club dinners) I must vote that porridge as my most enjoyed meal After this, as it was getting dark, I went home, but not before my red-moustached friend had secured a promise from me to come again next day to help him with his work. After about a week of wood-splitting, we went together to the Commandant's base, where I achieved my ambition of "joining up" in the so-called Labour Battalion, consisting for the most part of men and boys too young or otherwise unsuitable for active service. The very first night, walking on air, I went to my diggings, where my landlady had nearly given me up for lost. So, in my new uniform, shortened in most parts, I sat at the table, a guest of honour; all the simple souls asking me if I had a rifle. "No," I said carelessly, "but I can have one for the asking, as my friend is an officer; for hasn't he two stripes on his coat-sleeve?" But I must confess that my work was anything but easy. Here is the programme · up at 5 a m, in pitch darkness, light the kitchen fire, and put some stone-hard white bread to thaw; men's breakfast at 6-30 consisting of bacon, tea and biscuits. A privileged few, including Corporal Preston, the cook and myself had white bread—for with true philosophy the corporal said that as there wasn't enough to go round, we might as well have it all! After breakfast we had general parade in the snow, then most of the men went off to the aerodrome, and I got on with my wood-splitting, interrupted only by fierce guerilla with the night sentries, who, strangely enough wanted to sleep. In these arguments I was outclassed, but Corporal Preston always came to my rescue. I might mention that Corporal Preston had seen many years of service at sea He also kept a public-house at Bristol; so the enemy used to retire hastily before his eloquence. After this I had to fill up many water urns. For water I had to go some 100 yards out in the river, as nearer than that to the shore it was frozen to the bottom I invariably filled the buckets too full, with the result that each evening I had to be thawed out of my trousers In the evening I had my daily lesson in English as, sneaking to the men's quarters (I was none too welcome here, owing to my wood chopping operations) I listened to their talk and songs (To be continued) P.N K Corporal Preston Corporal Preston R.F.C. corporal in the story; had served at sea and kept a public-house at Bristol P.N. K P.N K sign-off initials P.N K Russia Bristol

items.sum: Mock letter from "turf commission agents" teasing "Observer" and "Tipster" over betting odds for the club's Ten and Twenty Miles Walking Championships (Murphy and Ricketts Shields).
e: Ten and Twenty Miles Walking Championships
items.s: CORRESPONDENCE. Mock letter from "turf commission agents" teasing "Observer" and "Tipster" over betting odds for the club's Ten and Twenty Miles Walking Championships (Murphy and Ricketts Shields). Tatt's Ring, Newmarket. To the Editor of The Belgravian 17th October, 1928. Dear Sir, Although speculation as to the identity of " Observer " has been rife amongst your readers for some while past, we must confess that whilst, as Turf Commission Agents, we found his paragraphs interesting and pertinent, we were but mildly bitten with curiosity concerning him until yesterday, when your October issue reached us. Then, when anxiously pondering over the newly-arisen query, "Whoever can 'Tipster' be?" we remembered the suggestion made by one of our most respected clients in a previous issue of The Belgravian respecting "Observer," and immediately the thought flashed into our minds: "Why! 'Tipster' is surely 'Observer,' but the poor dear old lady must have either lost his glasses or taken several more than are good for him!" We sincerely hope that this suspicion is correct, since there is one alternative that is by no means pleasing. For is it not possible that in "Tipster" you have amongst you one who contemplates " making a book" when the Ten and Twenty Miles Walking Championships are decided; and who hopes, by dwelling in your Magazine upon the very real brilliance of a great many of your stars, that those of you who like to indulge in an occasional flutter may be induced to overlook other stars, that threaten to out-shine the ones whose dazzling has been commented upon? Before now herrings have been drawn across the trail by astute old foxes who were desirous of throwing dust into the eyes of their pursuers, leading them up the garden, and fleecing them to a cinder. (Our meaning, we believe, is quite clear, Mr. Editor; so please pardon us if, in our agitation, we mix our metaphors). Should this prove to be the case, and should the identity of "Tipster" be established, all who do business with him would do well to first make a point of inquiring what odds he is prepared to lay against each of those who, he states, "Should fight out the Championships between them." If in the "Murphy Shield" race he quotes very short prices regarding Tommy Green, Harold King, R. D. McMullen and J. G. Scamell, he will be left with practically no choice but to give tens at the very least against a mere sorry cab-ranker, such as A. L. Fletcher. Then, when the distination of the "Ricketts Shield" is to be settled upon, if "Tipster" did not welsh during the earlier race, he should be given the opportunity of quoting short prices concerning Green, McMullen, Cooper and King. When he has done so ,the would-be better should be able to procure very favourable terms if his idle fancy prompts him to back a horse which is, presumably, but a negligible creature when judged according to its achievements (does not "Tipster" wholly disregard it?) but which nevertheless appeals to him strongly, simply because in "Fred Rickards" it has a name which strikes him as being extraordinarily "winsome." He will, at least, have good reason to expect longer odds against these two horses from "Tipster" than he is at all likely to obtain from Yours faithfully, The Reliable "Old Firm" of H. AND I. CAPPER. Tommy Green Tommy Green named as a fancied walker for the Murphy Shield Harold King Harold King named as a fancied walker for the Murphy Shield R. D. McMullen R. D. items.label: November 1928
items.sum: H. Parker's letter replying to "H." on the identity of the columnist "Observer", suggesting he is a recent member from north of the Thames.
items.s: A REPLY TO " H." H. Parker's letter replying to "H." on the identity of the columnist "Observer", suggesting he is a recent member from north of the Thames. 3, Artillery Row Buildings, S.W.1. Dear H, I am rather surprised that you, whilst complaining of the anonymity of "Observer," should yourself hide behind a nom de plume. Why not come out into the open? I myself, with many others, am intrigued as to the identity of "Observer." I am not "Observer." (And perhaps our old friend Nobby Clark put the reason into a nutshell when he told me I had not the brains. Perhaps he is "Observer?" Who knows?) Neither do I know who "Observer" is (as such) As you suggest, he—or she—certainly seems to know quite a lot about running, and in going through "Observer's" notes, it has struck me that he knew more about Middlesex or North of Thames items of interest, than Surrey or South of Thames; therefore I have been looking amongst our recently-acquired members for this elusive individual. For I think he is a new-comer to the Club, and any old stager who knows the people about whom he has written in his potted biographies, would understand. I at one time thought he would be found as a frequent visitor to the track at the Duke of York's Then again, in "Observer's" notes in the September Magazine he gives us quite a lot of detail about a small meeting at Rayleigh on August Bank Holiday. This meeting, as far as I am aware, was not reported through the usual sporting channels. So how did he get his details of the happenings? Did he compete? Was he a visitor? Did he hear it in gossip. It certainly looks as if "Observer" almost unmasks himself. Perhaps this will help you to unravel the mystery. At one time I was looking for "Observer" amongst the flowers, but I have since altered my opinion, and will take a walk along the road to the cherry orchard, and see what luck I have! Yours sincerely, H. PARKER. H. Parker H. PARKER letter writer; address in the issue Nobby Clark Nobby Clark "our old friend"; club not stated (only "our old friend") Duke of York's Rayleigh

items.s: OUR OPEN WALK Report on Belgrave's Open Walk, with its record entry, C. W. Hyde's win on a short new course, Belgrave's dead-heat with Herne Hill Harriers for the team race, and the results and handicaps. When in November, 1927, we received an entry of 200 for our Open Walk, it appeared that a record had been achieved that might stand for a long while; yet for this year's event our programme showed 254 competitors, only 8 of whom were included in two teams. Thus there were 246 potential staters, comprising 28 teams and 25 individual entrants, and of this huge total 225 faced the starter. As an illustration of the recent growth in popularity of the sport of Road-walking, and in particular of this annual fixture of ours, the following figures are illuminating :— In 1924 we had 140 Entrants ,, 1925 ,, ,, 137 ,, ,, 1926 ,, ,, 133 ,, ,, 1927 ,, ,, 200 ,, 1928 ,, ,, 246 ,, In each of these years the support accorded to our race was surpassed only by that given to the Road Walking Association in its opening walk of the season and its Championships. This is as it should be. It is obviously the duty of every Club to compete in all the events organized by the bodies to which it is affiliated, and so, although we hope to cater for larger fields year by year, we also hope that the R.W.A. will still outstrip our records. The starters in its race at Bowes Park this year exceeded our number by 6 only. For such whole-hearted support our thanks are due to all walkers in the South of England. The race for individual honours revealed the fact that in C. W. Hyde the A.A.A. has a champion well worthy of the honour. He has won each of the three open races at seven miles held in the London district this season; and in doing so, he has defeated huge fields, including most of the fastest walkers in the country. Although winning our race by about 70 yards only, he led throughout, and his superiority was never in doubt. Unfortunately, we were compelled to choose a new course for this year's race on account of road dis-repairs, and thus we cannot estimate his ability by comparing his performance with that of G. R Goodwin when setting up our course record of 54mins. 9secs., in 1924. The new course was obviously not a full seven miles. The probability is that is was fully 700yds. short. For team honours the Herne Hill Harriers gave us a rare fight, their third and fourth men just beating our fourth man to dead-heat with us on points. J. E. e: Inter Club Walk (Belgrave Harriers v. Metropolitan Police)
items.s: INTER CLUB WALK Report and result of Belgrave's inter-club walk with the Metropolitan Police Athletic Association on December 8th, won by R. D McMullen, Belgrave winning by 28 points (the printed Police score includes position 24, which the result lists as a Belgrave man). With the Metropolitan Police Athletic Association, December 8th. The excellent team we fielded for this event contrasted extremely with the poor muster at Banstead. Apparently we are too lazy or prejudiced against Club walks away from Wimbledon to give them support. Our team victory, although on paper not overwhelming, was quite decisive on account of the consistent good form shown by those walkers who go out regularly on Saturdays from St. John's Hall Although, as usual, Scamell and Elson set the pace at the start, McMullen and Batson (of the Police) soon took the lead, popular "Mac" gradually getting away (he led by 30yds. at half-distance) to win handsomely by 60yds. from Batson. A short lap of the Common was added to our ' open" course to make up the required distance. Perhaps we had the advantage of being "at home" to the Police, who turned out in good numbers. We are grateful for their enthusiastic support On our side, A. L. Fletcher made a timely first appearance on the road this season, but we were again without T W Green, through temporary indisposition SCORES. items.s: CLUB JUNIOR ROAD-WALKING CHAMPIONSHIP. Report and result of the club's fourth annual junior seven-mile road-walking championship for the Horwood Cup, won by F Elson, with the sealed handicap. The result of this, the fourth annual race over seven miles for the Horwood Cup, previously held by J. G. Scamell (twice) and A. L Fletcher, showed few surprises. In a well-fought race, J. E. Field made a good effort in the hope of catching F Elson, but the latter did not falter. J Rathbone who, one thinks, should have a place in this championship, looked like making an impression on the leaders at one time, but they were hard nuts to crack ! C. H. Speechley gave his best show since coming back from the States, whilst E. Saunders was the only competitor to find an "off" day All the others showed remarkable improvement on their figures of the previous Saturday, against the police, over the same course. This rate of progress must be maintained until we have the R.W.A. trophy in our possession. It was very satisfactory that the first six men shared the medals and the prizes in the sealed handicap between them. Actual Time H'cap Net Time Pos in H'cap 1 F Elson 58 45 0 40 58 5 4 2 J. items.sum: Report and results of the Surrey Walking Club's Croydon to Banstead and back walk, won by H W. Kemp, where Belgrave beat Valentines S.C. for second team place.
items.s: ANNUAL CROYDON TO BANSTEAD AND BACK RACE. Report and results of the Surrey Walking Club's Croydon to Banstead and back walk, won by H W. Kemp, where Belgrave beat Valentines S.C. for second team place. This race does not find favour with most of our men on account of the length and hilly nature of the 11¾ miles course Strange objections to be found in a Club holding the National Road Walking Championship! However, the tales one hears about "Banstead" are really absurd as, tackled steadily, the walk can be enjoyed even by a novice. Our reputation was saved by those top-class men, F. Rickards and R. D. McMullen. The other four of our team walked up to form and enabled us, much to our relief, to beat the Valentines S.C. for second place in the team contest. The introduction of that Club to the fixture is to commended, especially as we unfortunately do not give proper support. Such a sporting affair deserves better attention than we have given it this year and we owe it to our cordial hosts of the occasion, the Surrey Walking Club, to turn out a representative team, even if some of our boys are mistaken enough to miss one of the best fixtures on our card ! items.s: WALKING NOTES Walking notes on Cambridge Harriers handicap entries, the Surrey W.C. Croydon to Godstone and back Boxing Day walk (Belgrave second team), new walkers and recruiting. Entries for the Cambridge H 7 miles Road Handicap on the 19th inst should reach the walking secretary not later than Friday, the 11th inst, so that teams may be made up. In the Surrey W C's Open Croydon to Godstone and back walk on Boxing Day, we were not so strongly represented as we had hoped, but all the members of our team walked splendidly, and we were second in the team race, 6 points behind the promoting Club. The trying weather conditions tested the stamina of the walkers, many of whom were exhausted over the last few miles. R D. McMullen again made his mark. He has now been, at different times, 1st, 2nd and 3rd in this annual race. Jack Carne's was a gallant performance. 65 started Several new members of this section, S. Ring, A. Scott, F. H. Elson and H H. Norman, have been well up in recent novices' walks Although numerically we are stronger than most Clubs there is room for a great many more walkers in our ranks. items.s: BOXING DAY. Report and results of the club's Boxing Day meeting: a 120 yards handicap, a two miles handicap won by W. Rice and a three miles walk won by C. W. Redgrave. Despite continuous rain, fields were quite good for the three races at our annual gathering, and spectators were there in force. Inches only decided between the finalists in the sprint. Not all who entered this race carried their intentions further, so that a casual observer might have wondered why heats were not made up on the day from those present only. The competitors did not run in strings and the fact that several cross-country runners were competing (with the two miles to follow), gave the race an old-time atmosphere, when most men on the Belgrave programme competed in all the events, sprints, distance and walk! In the two miles run Jack Flower, on scratch, soon showed his intention of getting through the big field. Bill Rice, when the scratch man caught him, displayed a similar ambition and they were still together on the last lap. George Still was well placed at this time and, knowing the necessity, he speeded-up well for an "old 'un." Rice began to get the better of his argument with Flower and then overtook the leaders in style to win by a good margin from Flower. A. Traquair made good use of his mark to get third. There was special applause for G. Still, who was close behind, ran well for a veteran. Ken O'Kell, our ex-champion from Stoke, came to revive old acquaintance and turned out in this event. Walking in excellent style, C. W. Redgrave won the walk by a distance from A. W. Godfrey (who was second when last this Boxing Day race was held). Len Fletcher (scr) was in good form, and walked fourth. RESULTS 120yds. Handicap—W. B. Haymond (8yds.), 1; G. R. Maryon (5½yds.), 2, J. S. Williams (8yds.), 3. Time 12 1-5 secs. Two Miles Handicap—W. items.label: December 1928
items.sum: Report and results of the club 7 mile cross-country championship for the Blackstaffe Shield at Wimbledon on December 22nd, won by E. A. Duffett from A. Allum, who won the sealed handicap.
items.s: CROSS COUNTRY. Report and results of the club 7 mile cross-country championship for the Blackstaffe Shield at Wimbledon on December 22nd, won by E. A. Duffett from A. Allum, who won the sealed handicap. The Club 7 Mile C. C. Championship for the "Blackstaffe Shield," presented to the Club in 1910 by the old Olympian Sculling Champion, Mr. H. T. Blackstaffe, Club President 1909—1912, was decided over a new course at Wimbledon on December 22nd, and incidentally, by the exigencies of our fixture list, for the second time in 1928. That a strange fate has decreed that no member shall hold this trophy for more than two seasons was again evident when A. Clark, winner in 1926-27 and 1927-28, resigned his interest and did not compete. Other notable absentees were J. E. Flower, who was strongly fancied as a likely winner; W. S. Mitchell, who is apparently not keen on testing himself in a Club Championship; A. D. Pyer, nursing an ankle; and K. B. O'Kell, a previous dual winner and now "up north." No time was lost at the start and at a fast pace Duffett, Allum and Rice made the pace to the village and across the Golf course, followed by Klophin, W. S Webb and Robertshaw Down Gravelly Hill and along the Horse-ride to the Flagstaff, thence to the Windmill and the Village, which marked the end of the first lap, the course continued, and at the latter point Duffett and Rice turned together, with Allum but a yard behind . Then came Klophin, W S Webb and Robertshaw Harley, towards the rear, hesitated to stop or continue and eventually went on, but Phillips had failed to come into sight when a move was made for the finish and was the only one of 26 not timed in. Meantime Duffett and Allum continued the tussle. Rice faltered and finding the hills a sore test, dropped back and resigned third position to W. S. Webb, who was now running very strongly Klophin continued to run well, but was being dropped by the leaders; Robertshaw was showing a welcome return to form. T. J. Flower did not appear unduly pressed. Footer was running under difficulties and possibly unwisely but, let it be said, gallantly, whilst Penny did not appear uncomfortable all the way and never seemed likely to justify his "Junior" running. So to the field at the finish. Duffett and Allum hove into sight, and gave promise of a very close fight for premier honours. Duffett, however, had the necessary finishing speed, and eventually ran out a worthy and popular winner by a margin of a few yards. The form shown was, on the whole, quite satisfactory and augurs well for the forthcoming "Open" Championships Allum's running in particular was very good and this gained him first place in the Sealed Handicap by a comfortable margin. e: Inter-Club Run (Belgrave Harriers v. St. George's Services and London Scottish)
items.s: INTER-CLUB RUN. Report and results of the 4¾-mile inter-club run against St. George's Services and London Scottish A.C. from Hill Farm, Mitcham, on December 8th, 1928, won by W. Lawton, with Belgrave winning the team match, 41 points to St. George's 48 and London Scottish 110. Versus St. George's Services and London Scottish A.C. Over 4¾ miles, on December 8th, 1928. From St. George's Headquarters at Hill Farm, Mitcham, the Clubs turned out as follows : St. George's 8, London Scottish 6, and Belgrave H. 12, so 6 a side scored. A fast start saw Lawton, the Grenadier Guardsman who was running for St. George's, and Tebbutt of S.L.H., who was representing the London Scottish, well in the lead, followed by Pyer and Bayliss. After 2 miles had been covered Duffett joined the leaders, while Bayliss had dropped a few places. The same positions were maintained to the finish. Lawton drawing away from Tebbutt to win by about 30yds. with Duffett, who had gone ahead of Pyer, the same distance away third. Our boys, as usual, packed well, and so enabled the Club to gain another victory. The feature of the race was vested in a fellow-Guardsman of Lawton's, who ran although not counting, and finished only a few yards behind his comrade. Times and positions are as under :— 1. W. items.h: "A" TEAM RACE WITH ROYAL AIR FORCE, KENLEY, AT KENLEY.
items.sum: Report and result of the "A" team's race against the Royal Air Force at Kenley on December 24th, won by J. E. Flower, with Belgrave winning by one point, 27 to 28.
items.s: "A" TEAM RACE WITH ROYAL AIR FORCE, KENLEY, AT KENLEY. Report and result of the "A" team's race against the Royal Air Force at Kenley on December 24th, won by J. E. Flower, with Belgrave winning by one point, 27 to 28. On Saturday, December 24th, our "A" team's fixture with the Royal Air Force turned out to be a most exciting struggle, and not an easy race, as we were led to expect. The race was held in a very isolated spot, and to make matters worse, the majority of our boys ran in spikes, although two-thirds of the way was on stony ground. Thanks mainly to J. E. Flower and W. Mitchell gaining the first two places for us, we just managed to win by one point, although the Air Force boys finished their scoring five in the first eight places; our five finished in ten. The race itself was very interesting. At the start W. Mitchell and J. E. Flower soon worked their way to the front, accompanied by Corporal Whale, and then gradually drew further and further away from the rest of the field, and in a close finish, our boys just got the better of the airman. C. Strange's was an improved performance and, as you will see by the result, it was a good job for us he found his best form that day. I take this opportunity of thanking T. Curley for his help in getting the results and sending them to the Press; it was not a very thankful job on such a day. I also would like to thank the Royal Air Force for a jolly good tea which they placed before us, including sansage and mash, and I hope we will be able to give them as good a time when we have our return fixture with them at Wimbledon. 1.
