items.sum: Treasurer's reminder to members to pay overdue subscriptions, social debts and the Belgravian's quarterly shilling.
items.s: THE LAST LAP. Treasurer's reminder to members to pay overdue subscriptions, social debts and the Belgravian's quarterly shilling. We have now entered the final quarter of the Club's financial year, and I regret that some members have not yet paid their subscriptions. Will those members kindly send me a remittance by return of post? Surely nine months is time enough in which to remember to pay your dues? Also certain members have liabilities to our Social Hon Sec, and I should be pleased to hear that he has received these overdue payments. Perhaps the most unfortunte sufferer in this laxity in payment is "The Belgravian." When did you last pay our Editor any cash? Remember it is only a shilling a quarter, and being such a small amount, it gets sadly forgotten (but not by the Editor, who has to meet the bills). Now make a point of paying a shilling to Mr. Harley the very next time you see him; or, better still, post it off to him now at 44 Rosebury Road, Fulham, S.W.6. Finally, please remember that financial liability to the Club excludes entries for the Club Championships. A. E. MACHER, Hon. Treasurer. A. E. Macher A. E. MACHER Hon. items.label: August 1929
items.sum: Club notes on retaining the Jockey Cup, T. W. Green's win in the Birmingham Outer Circle 25 miles walk, new members, the Brighton Walk, B. W. Hayman's illness and the coming Annual General Meeting.
items.s: Club notes on retaining the Jockey Cup, T. W. Green's win in the Birmingham Outer Circle 25 miles walk, new members, the Brighton Walk, B. W. Hayman's illness and the coming Annual General Meeting. The Club's thanks and congratulations are due to Messrs. Webb, Penny, Rice and Flower (T. J.) for the part they played in retaining the "Jockey" Cup for the Club sideboard. Their positions at the finish (4, 5, 6 and 7) are indicative of the fine team-spirit which is helping Belgrave to success, and is an example of co-operative effort, which is deserving of commendation and imitation. * * * * * We extend our heartiest congratulations also to T. W. Green on his splendid achievement in winning the twenty-five miles road walk round the Birmingham Outer Circle. This walk was contested by all the prominent distance-walkers and a glance at the names of the men who followed Tommy home (T. Lloyd Johnson, 2nd; J. Medlicott, 3rd; F. Smith, 4th) is in itself adequate testimony to the merit of our man's performance. * * * * * This month A. E. Saward, A. W. Sime, J. G. Barrett, J. W. Harris, H. E. Wills, G. E. J. Plummer, T. E. Daley, H. Hewison, E. G. Andrews, H. G. Leslie, M. P. Whitlock and R. Herring join our ranks and are cordially welcomed. Two of the above have already distinguished themselves : Saward, by winning our hurdles handicap and Daley, by being placed in a recent novice race promoted by the Metropolitan W.C.; whilst Harold Wills, who is a first-claim member to our friends and rivals, Herne Hill Harriers, is already well-known to many of us. * * * * * The Brighton Walk will take place on September 14th and we expect to be strongly represented and hope to regain the team trophy which Surrey W.C. took from us last year. Our Hon. Walking Secretary would be pleased to hear from any members or friends who are willing to accompany the walkers as attendants. Many of our members with cycles have rendered invaluable assistance in the past and it is hoped that their help, which is always greatly appreciated, will again be forthcoming on this occasion. Those able to assist should communicate with MR. O. HORWOOD, 13 Abbott Avenue, S.W.20. We shall have a 'bus, as usual, on the road, and application for seats (5/-) should be made promptly. We are pleased to be able to announce that B. W. Hayman, who has been seriously ill and undergone many operations, is now a little easier and, whilst he is not entirely out of danger, his gradual recovery may be confidently expected. Hayman, who won our Boxing Day sprint and has since showed himself to be one of our fastest juniors, was actually representing the Club two days before he was taken ill. We are sure we are voicing the sentiments of all our readers when we wish him a quick return to normal health and fitness. * * * * * The Club Annual General Meeting will take place on September 24th at a hall which will be advised later. It is hoped that every member who can attend will do so and exercise his right of electing capable officials for the forthcoming Club year. items.label: August 1929
items.sum: Article by "Meander" picking out the Belgrave runners and walkers whose styles are worth imitating.
items.s: SOME OF THE BELGRAVE STYLISTS. Article by "Meander" picking out the Belgrave runners and walkers whose styles are worth imitating. One frequently notices that members of certain Clubs adopt different styles of running. For example : one observes that South London Harriers' men are mostly very long striding—especially over the country—and the Fitzroy Lodge runners have a fine track action, due no doubt to the interest that the world's best half-miler takes in them. But, as far as one can tell, Belgravians are not turned out in one pattern, and on the whole they are more successful than they are graceful to watch. I will now proceed to discuss one or two of our runners whose styles are worthy of imitation. Perhaps the best of our sprinters, from the point of view of easiness and grace of movement, is T. H. Needs, a veteran. It can be seen that he is still very neat and quick out of the holes and that he always keeps his form to the end of the sprint. For middle distance running, I do not think many will quarrel with giving the palm to J. A. Jones. There are few men running to-day who make running look so easy as does this most promising athlete. Jones is very careful and conscientious in training and, being gifted with an almost perfect action and a very strong finish, there is no reason why in a few years he should not become the most famous of Belgravians on the track. For the mile, I venture to differ completely from "Observer" and say that T. H. Scrimshaw has the style that is more adaptable to this distance than the half. Half-milers nowadays tend to be of the quarter type and although Scrimshaw has gained our quarter standard medal I think with his quicker (rather than long) stride and light build he could be the ideal mile runner. W. G. Webb was once spoken of by a former world-record holder as having the most correct action possible for cross-country running, and, as will be remembered, my friend "Observer"—whoever he might be—said that he is a mystery man, the mystery being how he can cover the ground in so effortless a fashion. He has a long easy stride and carries his arms low down. If any young runner wants his heart broken, he should ask our Cross Country Captain to take him round for what he (Webb) regards as a slow lap. The above discussion has been written more from the point of view of distance, and in consequence no mention so far has been made of the Flowers. But in any Belgrave article appreciating style they ought to be mentioned. T. J., the elder, has a long raking stride—to quote my friend again—which is partly due to his length of leg and partly to cultivation. Any very tall runner would profit by imitating our mile champion. J. E. has a slightly more easy action than his brother, and it seems suitable for almost any distance, from the half upwards. Coming to the walkers; I must say that there is no other Club which encourages track walking to the same extent, nor which has so large a proportion of good stylists. Those who watch open walks and are liable to be disgusted with the rolling gait and running on heels that one sees, should watch a Belgrave handicap. They will see one of the finest walkers in the country—both for performance and action—on the scratch mark; but what is more remarkable, they will see the young front-markers walking in faultless fashion and without any of the movements that rightly make the crowd laugh. Of the younger walkers, the best are H. J. Fletcher—whose style is every bit as good as that of his famous brother—L. Storey, R. F. Elson and C. W. Redgrave. C. R. Strange, before he deserted the walking ranks, also looked good. On the road we seem to be almost unbeatable as far as performance is concerned, but the only walkers I would care to recommend as patterns would be H. F. King, who changed and improved his style two years ago, and J. E. Field. For absolutely fair walking, as was said in a recent number of "The Belgravian," A. H. East's is as near perfection as possible. So must conclude this dissertation on the Belgrave stylists, and it is hoped that their numbers will steadily increase, for there can be very few things more pleasing to the eye, or more lasting in the memory, than the sight of a stylist, whether he be runner or walker, annexing a championship. items.s: THE JUNIOR INTER-CLUB CONTEST. Report of the junior inter-club contest at Croydon on July 9th, won by Belgrave against Mitcham and Croydon, with a note on the Croydon Business Houses Relay. On July 9th, at Croydon, the Junior Inter-Club contest between Croydon, Mitcham and ourselves took place, Epsom failing to put in an appearance. The first event, 3 at 100yds., resulted in an easy win by 6yds for the Bels. Our team was A. E. Powter, V. L. Pemberton and J. S. Williams. In the 880yds. team race, 4 to run and 3 to score, our boys were T. H. Scrimshaw, J. E. Tosh, J. G. Coleman and T. C. Jones. Tom Scrimshaw made the pace at the start and Tosh came up to him 300yds. from home. They then commenced to amble in, but Charman, of Mitcham, came with a burst and our boys had to sprint home, crossing the finishing line together. Our team scored 1, 2, 4, with Jones filling 7th position, and so we won handsomely from Mitcham (17pts.) and Croydon (24pts.). The last Junior event was 3 at 200yds., and B. W. Hayman gave us a lead of 10yds. over the first stage. V. L. Pemberton increased our advantage, and Jack Williams broke the worsted well ahead of Mitcham, who were closely followed by Croydon. An interesting feature of this meeting was the Croydon Business Houses Relay, in which one of our members, S. R. Chorley, represented his firm, who finished 3rd in the race. A. E. Powter A. E. items.label: August 1929
items.h: DOUBLE WIN v. ST. GEORGE'S S.S.C. AND MITCHAM A.C.
items.sum: Report of Belgrave winning both the junior relay and the two miles team race at a St. George's Services S.C. meeting on July 15th.
items.s: DOUBLE WIN v. ST. GEORGE'S S.S.C. AND MITCHAM A.C. Report of Belgrave winning both the junior relay and the two miles team race at a St. George's Services S.C. meeting on July 15th. On July 15th, at a meeting organised by St. George's Services S.C., we participated (with Mitcham A.C.) in two events, a junior (under 19) relay, 6 x 880yds., and a two miles team race, which served as a trial to select the team to defend the "Jockey" Cup on the following Saturday. Our junior relay team ran in the following order : T. C. Jones, W. Jacobs, J. G. Coleman, R. Barsby, J. E. Tosh and T. H. Scrimshaw. Jones gained a useful lead over the first St. George's runner, but as Mitcham A.C. had only five runners present, they joined in at the first change-over and started level with our second man. This was Jacobs, the youngest of our team, and he was unlucky in that he had to run against the strongest men of the opposing two teams. He lost ground over the latter part of his stage, but this was partly recovered by Coleman. Barsby followed, losing ground, but Jim Tosh not only pegged the others back, but handed over with a thirty yards lead, which Scrimshaw, running comfortably, increased to eighty yards over the Mitcham A.C. boy, with St. George's S.C. still farther back. The juniors, having in this manner maintained the Belgrave prestige, it was now the turn of the seniors. In the two miles race, six a side ran, scoring four each. The Belgrave team went away from the rest of the field, in company with Coe, of St. George's, and Ferdinando, of Mitcham, and eventually finished in the following order : 1, W. A. Rice; 2, T. J. Flower; 3. A. Penny; 4, E. A. Duffett; 5, A. Allum; 6, Ferdinando (Mitcham A.C.); 7, A. H. Coe (St. George's S.S.C.); 8, H. E. Footer. It will be seen that we finished the first five men. items.h: BELGRAVE JUNIORS v. OLD GAYTONIANS A.C.
items.sum: Report and results of the Belgrave juniors' match with the Old Gaytonians at Harrow on July 18th, lost by three events to two.
items.s: BELGRAVE JUNIORS v. OLD GAYTONIANS A.C. Report and results of the Belgrave juniors' match with the Old Gaytonians at Harrow on July 18th, lost by three events to two. In beautiful weather, amidst glorious surroundings, the juniors decided their match with the Old Boys of the Gayton School, on the school ground at Harrow, on July 18th. It was originally decided that 10 juniors should represent the Bels., so as not to call upon juniors to race twice, but owing to the absence of Hayman and Ford, through illness, Scrimshaw and Tosh were called upon to compete in two events. The first race to be decided was the 440yds. J. V. Powell, the L.A.C. runner, went into the lead which he kept all the way; Scrimshaw, slowing down in the last 10yds., nearly lost second place, just making a dead-heat of it with H. Whitmill. First blood to Gayton. The next event was the 100yds., in which we had a great misfortune. J. S. Williams was slightly in the lead at 70yds. when he caught his feet in the ground and fell heavily. Thus another event went to Gayton. The third race gave us a win. This event, the 880yds., saw Tosh in good form and, after holding off R. H. Gowar, he had a comfortable win. The Relay race gave the Bels. their second win. Scrimshaw took the "half" and, running a brainy race with Gowar, sent Pemberton away with a nice lead. Powter then took over and, keeping well away from the Gaytonian, handed over to Tosh who, running strongly over the last 440yds. won by 40yds. Score 2 all. The Long Jump decided the match and, despite lack of practice, the Bels. put up a good show, being only beaten by 5 feet. After the match the Gayton Club entertained the juniors with coffee and sandwiches. Mr. Atkinson (A.A.A.) then said how delighted he was with the sport provided by our boys and hoped to see us again next year. Scrimshaw, our captain, suitably replied and called upon the Bels. for three cheers for the Gaytonians, which were lustily given. RESULTS. 440 Yards—1, J. V. Powell, O.G.A.C.; 2, T. H. items.label: August 1929
items.sum: Report of Belgrave retaining the Jockey Cup team race ahead of Herne Hill and Surrey A.C., with a second team placed second in a three miles team race at the Ponder's End meeting the same afternoon.
items.s: THE "JOCKEY" CUP RETAINED. Report of Belgrave retaining the Jockey Cup team race ahead of Herne Hill and Surrey A.C., with a second team placed second in a three miles team race at the Ponder's End meeting the same afternoon. Last year our boys were successful in winning the "Jockey" Cup, so gaining the Club's first victory in open team races, and for this reason our runners were particularly keen to retain the trophy this year. This they did rather easily, winning from Herne Hill Harriers by no less than 12 points. Our team packed very well and showed the spectators team-racing in the fullest sense of the word by finishing as follows : W. G. Webb, 4; A. W. Penny, 5; W. A. Rice, 6; T. J. Flower, 7. The final result was :— Our strength in distance runners was exemplified by the fact that on the same afternoon another team gained second place in a three miles open team race at the Ponder's End meeting. This team consisted of E. A. Duffett, 5; H. E. Footer, 7; W. S. Mitchell, 11; A. Allum, 15; with F. W. Jude, whose fine Marathon running is still fresh in our memories, as fifth man. Watford H. won this race from our team by 7 points. So it will be seen that on the anniversary of the winning of the first open team race on the track, our winners came very near to winning two open team races in one afternoon; but this is a pleasure that must be deferred a little longer. 1. items.label: August 1929
items.h: THE SOUTHERN AMATEUR ATHLETIC LEAGUE 4 x 880 YARDS RELAY.
items.sum: Report of Belgrave finishing fourth in the Southern Amateur Athletic League 4 x 880 yards relay at Battersea Park on July 24th, and losing the Winstone Trophy relay to Surrey A.C. the same evening.
items.s: THE SOUTHERN AMATEUR ATHLETIC LEAGUE 4 x 880 YARDS RELAY. Report of Belgrave finishing fourth in the Southern Amateur Athletic League 4 x 880 yards relay at Battersea Park on July 24th, and losing the Winstone Trophy relay to Surrey A.C. the same evening. This event took place on July 24th at Battersea Park, and we were represented by T. H. Scrimshaw, W. A. Rice, T. J. Flower and J. A. Jones, running in that order. Tom Scrimshaw started well for us, holding Hedges (S.L.H.) and Picton (Poly H.), two long-striding runners, until the last few yards. He handed over third about six yards behind Hedges to Bill Rice. Bill held the position, but Surrey A.C. came up and Poly H. dropped behind us. This order was maintained over the next stage and Jack Jones started off third with Booth, the Poly champion, a few yards behind him. Booth passed Jack in the concluding stages, and so we finished fourth. Surrey A.C. won the race, profiting by a blunder on the part of one of the S.L.H. men, who had dropped the baton and so lost fifteen yards, with our team about forty yards out, filling fourth position. On the same evening we were paid a very high compliment by Surrey A.C., who sent their strongest relay team (Griffiths, Higgins, Wigzell and Dacombe) to wrest from us the "Winstone" Trophy which we won last year at Hook. We were represented by Tosh, J. S. Williams, Titherley and Dunckley, not our strongest team by any means, two of the team being still under nineteen, and were beaten by 25yds. Our men were not disgraced in losing to such a strong combination, and we derive greater satisfaction from the subtle compliment paid us than we would have done in winning the trophy ourselves from trifling opposition. items.label: August 1929
items.sum: Report of the last Inter-Club Relays meeting, held at Epsom on July 31st, at which Belgrave retained the Inter-Club Relay Shield, with the final points table.
items.s: THE INTER-CLUB RELAYS—FINAL MEETING. Report of the last Inter-Club Relays meeting, held at Epsom on July 31st, at which Belgrave retained the Inter-Club Relay Shield, with the final points table. The last of the Inter-Club Relays, held at Epsom on July 31st, was decided in fine weather although it rained hard previous to the time of starting. It was this fact which doubtless caused our sprinters once more to fail us, only one—A. A. Lander—turning up. As Lander has had experience of cross-country running it will probably be as well for our sprinters to spend next season over the country and so prepare themselves for the vagaries of our summer climate. Our team for the 4 at 100yds. had an unfamiliar appearance, it being composed of Lander, Tosh, Scrimshaw and Duffett! To our surprise they managed to beat Epsom, Mitcham winning the event from Croydon in 43secs. The 4 at 880yds. resulted in an easy win for the “Bels.”, our team, (Bayliss, Scrimshaw, Rice and Tosh) ran well, and the lead given them by Bayliss was gradually increased. Tosh broke the tape a good 220yds. in front of the Mitcham boy, with Epsom surprisingly beating Croydon for third place. Our team for the 4 at 300 yds. was the same as for the 100’s, and as one of the number was due to run in the mile immediately following it was decided to run over and so secure the point for finishing. Mitcham gained a narrow victory over Croydon in this race, with Epsom a good way behind, third. The mile team race saw only three running for us, namely, Rice, Footer and Duffett, but as they finished in this order, 2, 3, 4, we, of course, won easily. Ferdinando, of Mitcham, ran a good race to win in 4min. 46secs., and his team finished second, with Croydon just beating Epsom for third position. The points at the close of the meeting were Mitcham 14, Belgrave 11, Croydon 9, Epsom 6, quite a good performance on our boys’ parts considering there were only seven of them to contest four events. Prior to this meeting we held a 10 point lead in this competition, and so we once again won the Inter-Club Relay Shield. Total points are :— This year’s competition showed a noticeable lack of interest on the part of our sprinters in the away fixtures, and we have to thank our distance men once more for “bringing the bacon home.” Croydon and Mitcham had a fine fight for second place and it was only at the final meeting that Mitcham gained the lead. Epsom, as usual, were the wooden-spoonists of the competition and seem to be gradually declining, a pity when one thinks of the old days of the Primrose and Rose Hoop wearers. items.label: August 1929
items.sum: Report and results of the Belgrave Harriers club Championship Meeting, with Tom Scrimshaw setting a Club 880yds. record and T. J. Flower a Club mile record, plus the club handicap results.
items.s: THE CHAMPIONSHIP MEETING. Report and results of the Belgrave Harriers club Championship Meeting, with Tom Scrimshaw setting a Club 880yds. record and T. J. Flower a Club mile record, plus the club handicap results. We were favoured with fine weather for our Championship Meeting and a very large crowd assembled to pay tribute to our athletes. We are very fortunate in having such a keen following and we may be sure that their best wishes are with Belgrave, when there are championships to be won, or other clubs to be met. The programme commenced as usual with the 100yds. championship, and here M. E. Odell won for the fifth time—a very fine sequence of performances. The under-15 championship was next decided and the final resulted in a very close race, there being inches only over the first three runners. The time, 12secs., is meritorious and the future of these boys will be watched with interest. J. Cooper Clark, owing to indisposition, was unable to defend his titles, and the 880yds. championship was won in the fastest time yet recorded by Tom Scrimshaw. W. Lowden, a young runner of promise, set a very hot pace over the first quarter, after which Scrimshaw took the lead, followed by H. Titherley. J. E. Tosh then came up, passing Titherley and finishing second, beaten by four or five yards. Thus two of our junior runners, still under nineteen, gained the first two places, and to Scrimshaw fell the honour of beating the Club record by two-fifths of a second. Truly a wonderful performance, and one which presages still more important honours for our youthful champion—and the runner-up. A. L. Fletcher, who was unable to walk last year owing to illness, regained the walking championship. He was content to take things rather easily as the time shows, and was followed in by B. J. T. Knifton, whose twenty miles races do not seem to have impaired his speed, and F. H. Elson. The 440yds. title was won by George Dunckley and any other result appeared impossible after his running in the recent A.A.A. championships. Perce Cook was second for the second time that afternoon, and A. A. Lander third. The time, 52 1-5secs., does not denote George’s best, but is a sound performance. In the Mile championship T. J. Flower retained his title and succeeded in knocking “two-fifths” off the Club record. Mitchell led the field at the end of the first lap, and at the conclusion of the second Bert Footer “jumped” the field and opened up a gap. Soon after this, Bill Rice and Joe Flower overhauled Bert and strode out together until ten yards from the tape, when Bill “cracked,” leaving Joe a worthy winner. Meanwhile, W. G. Webb had moved up to third place and so the race finished. The Junior (under 18) 220yds. championship was won by S. Garland in a close finish from R. C. Impett—the promise of youth again being in evidence in this race. Two of the four handicaps held were won by young runners still at school. F. H. C. White the winner of the 880yds. handicap, completed the distance from his mark in 1min. 57½secs—the fastest club handicap yet—and so showed himself to have more than average ability. The same applies to L. Fleming, who had earlier been placed second in the under-15 hundred yards championships, and now won the 75yds. handicap. The 120yds. hurdles handicap introduced us to a newcomer in A. E. Saward, who cleared the hurdles in stylish manner and fast time and shows promise of developing into a first-class hurdler. The three laps hurdle race—technically it is not a steeplechase owing to the absence of a water-jump—gave Arthur Allum, one of our cross-country stalwarts, a win, with the scratch man, H. S. Cook, second. To conclude—the feature of the meeting seemed to be the fine performances and great promise of our younger members. The general standard was high, many standard medals being awarded, and the entries very gratifying. To all those who were successful—our congratulations; to those who “also ran,” remember, “they also serve who only stand and wait,” and draw the moral from Tom Scrimshaw’s running as here laid down : CHAMPIONSHIPS RESULTS. 100 Yards—M. Running Secretary of the last Club Handicaps on August 21st and the Southern Amateur Athletic League 3 miles team race at Herne Hill on the 28th, with thanks to members for the season. The month of August sees the track season drawing to a close and the last Club Handicaps are being held on the 21st. There are races at the following distances: 100yds., 440yds., 1320yds. and a two miles walk. On the 28th at Herne Hill Track is the last Southern Amateur Athletic League fixture, namely, the 3 miles team race, 4 to run and score. This is where we should have a decided advantage over the other clubs, and should win. I should like to thank all members who have supported the Club events, also those who have turned out in Relay races, Inter-Club contests, etc. The Club has had a most successful season, and I feel sure many of our members are eagerly looking forward to the winter season to provide them with an attractive fixture list. items.label: August 1929
items.sum: Column by "Observer" on poor support for the Southern Amateur Athletic League and the importance of Club vests, with pen portraits of V. J. Peacock, A. L. Fletcher and T. Pritchard.
items.s: SPORTS JOTTINGS Column by "Observer" on poor support for the Southern Amateur Athletic League and the importance of Club vests, with pen portraits of V. J. Peacock, A. L. Fletcher and T. Pritchard. Is the Southern Amateur Athletic League the success it was anticipated it would be? I am afraid not. The Clubs that form the League, although the best in the South, do not seem to support it as was expected. Even at the first meeting one Club failed to put in an appearance, while at the second two Clubs were absentees, and at the third meeting only three Clubs turned out. At the present rate of appearances we shall see the last event being abandoned owing to the absence of competing clubs. When the league was first formed the cry of “No entry fees and no awards” was made on its behalf. Does the trend of events since mean that this does not meet with the approval of Southern athletes? It would certainly appear so, and seems to prove that the incentive to run for the love of the sport is not so great as some people, especially the non-active ones, would have us believe. I cannot stress too much the importance of new members to our Club securing Club vests. Not only is the new pattern very smart, but when one is training and a claret and gold vest makes its appearance you are at home with the wearer directly. Many of our new members wear white vests, and on a crowded track it is difficult to tell whether they are Belgrave members or not. So I say to all whom this concerns—secure a vest at once from Mr. Macher and I am sure you will do credit to it and to our Club. My next three Club members include two members of our walking section, as follows :— V. J. Peacock, a well-known Civil Service walker and one who has also met with success in Open and Club events. A very persevering athlete and a valued member of our Committee. Is a first-class conjuror and often delights our socials during the winter by his clever performance. A. L. Fletcher, our best man at track walking and the present Surrey County Champion, while he performed with distinction in the recent A.A.A. race. Has also walked very well on the road and has been successful in the County road-walking Championship. Of very slight build, he has done excellently in recent years, winning many Open and Club races and, being still quite young, should keep the Belgrave name prominently in the forefront of the Walking world for many years to come. T. Pritchard, a name well known in the Club since his two elder brothers have both been prominent performers for the Bels. Tom bids fair to be the best of all three, and should meet with success in the near future, having so far this season experienced bad luck in open races, although being placed in a Club event. Also runs over the country and shewed promise last year of developing into a useful team man. Macher Mr. Macher printed "Mr. Macher"; supplies Club vests V. J. Peacock V. J. items.sum: Diary of Belgrave members' performances at open and other meetings from July 10th to August 10th 1929.
items.s: ROUND THE MEETINGS. Diary of Belgrave members' performances at open and other meetings from July 10th to August 10th 1929. July 10th. On this day C. T. Pollard won both the 100yds. and 220yds. championships of the Metropolitan Police A.A. B. W. Fleming was third in the 100yds. race. July 13th. T. W. Green won the 25 miles walk round Birmingham in 3hr. 50min. 20sec., with T. Lloyd Johnson, a former National champion, second, two minutes behind. To quote The Sporting Life, “Green was remarkably fresh and finished strongly, but Johnson was leg weary.” Two successes were scored by our men at the Chiswick “General” meeting, A. A. Lander winning the 100yds. and J. A. Jones the 880yds. B. J. T. Knifton won an Open Walk at Luton, W. Pinnock was second in a 440yds. race at Bexley Heath and P. J. E. Cook filled a similar position in a 220yds. handicap at Dagenham. A relay team consisting of T. Scrimshaw, H. Titherley, J. S. Williams and B. Hayman were successful at Hounslow, chiefly owing to a fine “quarter” by Scrimshaw; and B. Fleming was placed second in the All England Police Long Jump Championship held at Sheffield. On the same afternoon at Cranleigh, H. E. Footer was second in a mile handicap and third in a three miles race. July 18th. West End Divisions, T. Pritchard, 880yds., 3rd. July 20th. In addition to the team race successes at Herne Hill and Ponders End this day, described elsewhere, H. L. Rollins, our Social Hon. Sec., was fourth in the Mile Open at the North London meeting, and H. V. Hoving won a mile race at Godalming. Other successes were those of D. E. Jordan (veterans’ 100yds) and J. Cade (1 mile walk) in the closed events at the “Printers’ ” meeting. July 24th. On this evening two of our members, P. J. E. Cook and W. G. Webb, were included in a Middlesex County team v. R.A.F., Uxbridge; and W. Mitchell won a 10 miles road race at Edgware in good time. July 25th. B. W. Fleming retained the Long Jump Championship of Suffolk. July 27th. L. G. Hickman won the Hampshire Two Miles Walk Championship, and J. E. Tosh was second in the 880yds. Championship. At the Fire Brigade Meeting, M. A. Gray was second in the 880yds. and H. L. Rollins third in the Mile. The special prizes awarded for the largest entries in the mile handicap and two miles walk handicap were both secured by Belgrave, Arthur Allum and J. Cade being the respective winners. At the Miller Hospital Sports H. E. Footer won the Mile, off the virtual scratch mark, 96yds.; and tried to double this success with a win in the sack race, but here he was disqualified for having his foot through a hole in the sack. Hard luck, Bert! August 3rd. Whilst the Club Championships were taking place, J. Cade was gaining second place in a mile walk at Herne Hill. August 5th. We now come to Bank Holiday, with its usual multiplicity of meetings. At Oxted it was “Footer” Day, Bert winning the mile (off scratch) and three mile handicaps, being second in the 880yds. handicap and third in the sack race. He also attempted the wheelbarrow race and obstacle race, but in this latter event was forced to give in to a balloon which obstinately refused to be inflated! Our Bert was awarded a special prize for the best performance of the day, and there is little doubt that if there had been one for the best entertainer present, he would have won that also. Jim Tosh won the half-mile from scratch, with Footer second, as previously mentioned, and J. G. Coleman third. The runners-up to Footer in the mile were Morrell and Coleman; and Coleman was also second in the sack race. In the scratch relay race another small trophy was gained for the Club by the following team : A. A. Harley, J. E. Tosh, W. A. Rice and T. F. Morrell, running in that order. At Maidenhead, A. H. Shannon had a double win in the sprints and at Rayleigh A. A. Lander was successful in the hundred yards. At Chiswick, S. H. Warboys ran exceedingly well to finish fourth in a ten miles road race considering that the first and second men were both international runners, and the third, our old friend H. S. Cook, is no mean performer. Here H. Titherley and G. Basford were second and third in the local 220yds race. At Sevenoaks, W. S. Mitchell finished fourth in a ten miles road handicap off scratch. Other successes were those of A. Allum, second in mile at Chertsey, P. J. E. Cook, third in 440yds. at Romford, and E. A. Duffett, second in local half-mile at Beckenham. August 10th. At the City of London Police Meeting, the Cooks scored a double. Charlie won the Veterans’ 100yds. as easily as he did last year, and Perce was successful in the 220yds. Handicap. A. H. Graygoss, walking in the colours of his first-claim club, the L.C.C. Trams S.C., was third in the walk. At Windsor, H. E. Footer won the two miles handicap and A. Allum, the half-mile. Allum was also second in the mile. The above returns show that the “Bels.” are doing as well as ever at open meetings and it is expected that there will be several more successes to be reported before the season ends. C. T. Pollard C. items.label: September 1929
items.sum: The new President thanks members for electing him, reviews the club's growth and prospects, and asks members to help the Executive, with his portrait.
items.s: OUR NEW PRESIDENT. The new President thanks members for electing him, reviews the club's growth and prospects, and asks members to help the Executive, with his portrait. Permit me, first of all, to thank the members for the great honour they have conferred on me; for it is indeed a great honour to be President of the Belgrave Harriers, especially at the period of our long career when, after many vicissitudes, we are unquestionably the most progressive athletic club in the country. Every month we are not only growing numerically, but are also adding fresh laurels to our already long list. We have a sturdy band of tried and reliable team-men, both in running and walking; on track, road and country; while our juniors have exceeded our most optimistic expectations. The same can be truthfully said of our field events section, which is a sturdy youngster of great promise Our prospects for the coming cross-country and road walking season were never brighter. And now a word for the Executive The greater the membership the more work is thrown on their shoulders and they would be grateful for the co-operation of members in making their "labour of love" as light as possible. Somebody—somewhere—has very truly said, "The only way to obtain happiness is in making others happy." Let us start making ourselves happy through the instrumentality of our Hon Treasurer and the Hon. Editor of our magazine. E. GORDON. OUR NEW PRESIDENT. E. Gordon E. GORDON new President

Congratulations to Dunckley upon his international selection and consequent wonderful running; to Green, upon his London—Brighton Walk victory, and many other impressive wins, to our three-mile team which won the Southern Amateur Athletic League Race (our first blood!) and to all those who were called upon to take part in the Inter-County Meeting At the September Committee meeting the following were admitted to the Club R. items.h: THE CLOSE OF THE TRACK SEASON.
items.sum: Report and results of the club's closing track meeting of the summer on August 21st: 100yds and 440yds handicaps, a 1,320yds race and a 2 miles walk.
items.s: THE CLOSE OF THE TRACK SEASON. Report and results of the club's closing track meeting of the summer on August 21st: 100yds and 440yds handicaps, a 1,320yds race and a 2 miles walk. August 21st saw the last of our summer meetings, and as in previous years it was a comparatively short programme, owing to early darkness. The events included, as is usual at our closing meeting, a race over 1,320yds. and one heard the customary query as to why such an unusual distance was run. Entries were more numerous than in the past, for this time of the year, which is no doubt due to our increased membership, as well as to the indefatigable efforts of our running Hon. Sec. The 100yds handicap was run in six heats and most of the heat winners were long markers. The final produced a close race the verdict being given to L. Fleming, a very young runnner who had previously brought himself to notice by winning the 75yds. handicap at our Championship Meeting About twenty competitors started in the "three-quarters" and the limit man, L. E. Fletcher, was soon joined by Strange These two held the lead for some time, but the field was gradually closing on them, and then Jim Tosh, running a very fast last quarter, came through the field followed by a bunch of short-markers, to win in fast time from M. A Gray, with J. G. Coleman third. Ford occupied his favourite position, fourth The time for this event is the best yet recorded for this distance at any of our meetings. Three heats were needed for the "quarter" and as the handicap was framed off G R. Dunckley, although he did not turn out, the times were on the fast side. In the final T. C. Jones just managed to hold the lead and win in the useful time of 50 4-5 secs. In the walk J Vigor retained the lead until entering the finishing straight, but was then passed, first by Dodkin, who has improved very much this season. and then by Storey, but he managed to finished third. P. Khlopin, who has left the ranks of the runners and become a devotee of walking, performed very creditably and should be a useful addition to the road-walking teams this winter. There was another "convert" in the race, but the Editor forbids me to comment on him; but I would like to point out that very few walking stars shone in their first few races. items.label: September 1929
items.sum: Belgrave won the final Southern Amateur Athletic League fixture, a 3 mile team race at Herne Hill Track on August 28th, and finished third in the league.
items.s: THE SOUTHERN AMATEUR ATHLETIC LEAGUE. Belgrave won the final Southern Amateur Athletic League fixture, a 3 mile team race at Herne Hill Track on August 28th, and finished third in the league. The final Southern Amateur League fixture was held at Herne Hill Track on August 28th. The event was the 3 mile team race, 4 to run and score, our team being H. E Footer, A. W. Penny, J. E Flower and W. S. Mitchell. Five Clubs competed, the only absentees being Highgate H. O'Connor, Poly H., forced the pace at the start with Weatherill and Stansbury, both of South London H., in close attendance Footer, who had for a mile been well in the rear, then came through with a rush and the leaders commenced to draw away from the rest of the field. Simmons, of Surrey A.C., was unfortunately spiked and had to retire, so his team mates also withdrew in view of the all-to-score arrangement. This was a pity as they were packing very well and it looked like being a close race. From this stage, a little over two miles, until the finish, the team race was always in our safe keeping and although Bert tried hard to split the two S.L.H. men, he was unable to do so, Stansbury winning by 10yds. from Weatherill, with Footer the same distance away, third. The time, 15min. 12sec., was distinctly good, there being quite a fair wind during the evening. Our men scored as follows: Footer 3rd, Penny 5th, Flower 6th, and Mitchell 8th, total 22 points. South London H were 2nd with 26pts., then came Polytechnic H. and Herne Hill H. The end of the season found us placed third in this league—a satisfactory result when the class of opposition is considered. Next year we should do better, for this season we did not always field our strongest teams. For example, the team which retained the Horsham Cup (4 x 440yds. relay) was much superior, both in personnel and training, to the one which did duty at the League race in April, although this team was placed third. Final placings are:— 1. Polytechnic H. 32 pts 2 South London H. 30 pts 3. Belgrave H 20 pts 4 Herne Hill H. Surrey A C. 11 pts. 6. Highgate H. 4 pts. H. E. Footer H. He was timed to run his stage in the 4 x 440yds. race (with a flying start) in 48 3-10secs. In the Medley Relay he ran last for England and was about 10yds. behind Stortz, the German who was fifth at the Amsterdam Olympiad, when he took over George cut down this lead and was only beaten by 3yds.—a wonderful effort (considering the opposition) and one which deservedly gained the large crowd's applause The British record for the 440yds. is 48 2-5secs., and was made by W Halswelle at Glasgow in 1908 If our man can reproduce his form again next season it should be within his powers to improve upon these figures. 31/8/29—On this day the following team—J. Cooper Clark, P. J. E. Cook, H Titherley and G. R Dunckley—retained the Horsham Chamber of Trade Cup for a 4 x 440yds relay, which we won for the first time last year. items.label: September 1929
items.sum: Account of the London to Brighton Walk, followed from the Belgrave supporters' bus, with T. W. Green's win over Holt, the club's first win of the Knott Shield, and a list of Belgrave members' earlier Brighton times.
items.s: THE BRIGHTON WALK Account of the London to Brighton Walk, followed from the Belgrave supporters' bus, with T. W. Green's win over Holt, the club's first win of the Knott Shield, and a list of Belgrave members' earlier Brighton times. Promptly to time, on the first stroke of seven of Big Ben, the walkers started on their Annual Trek to Brighton. The 3 Italians shared popularity with Green, our star hope, and Holt, the Yorkshire postman. The pace set by two of the Italian walkers was much too fast, and eventually told its tale long before Brighton was in sight Green, walking well within himself, took things quietly, with Fred Rickards in close attendance. The walk through London is a long monotonous affair, and when Green came in sight at Croydon he was a good way behind Holt. Here Green was given a good reception by the club supporters, who had taken advantage of the 'bus hired by the Club for the race. Encouragement was lavishly accorded to Green and Rickards. Rathbone came along next, walking quite comfortably and with lots of strength in hand. Manning and Wattam pleased the crowd, as also did Bidgood. Fletcher came along in the last group, smiling and determined. Having seen all that was wanted, the 'bus continued its journey. Going through Purley the supporters started picking up the Club members and vocal assistance was given to our men. Speechley was noticed by his frantic efforts to catch the eyes of the attendants, as he wanted a drink. Arriving amongst the leaders we found that Rickards had now got level with Green and both were walking well. At Mitcham the 'bus arrived first, followed by Holt, who was well ahead of the field. Green and Rickards were still a good way behind, but well within striking distance of the leaders. The next point of vantage for the supporters was Crawley and here we had a great time. Holt had been forced to stop outside Crawley, and Green, taking advantage of this, left Rickards and went out to open a gap between himself and Holt A "movie-talkie" machine had been erected at this point When the news came through that Green would be first through Crawley the supporters gathered round the machine and gave Green a great reception The talkie, if ever released for the public, will prove the vocal powers of some of the Belgraves. Rickards at this stage was none too bright and Rathbone had found trouble. Manning, Wattam and Bidgood were progressing well, while Martin was walking gingerly owing to hip trouble Vic Winner had now retired. After leaving Crawley we had a minor shock, for Green was having a bad time and Holt caught him on the long drag up-hill to Handcross Here Holt had a lead of about two minutes and was walking stronger than Green, who was coming round after his bad time From here to Bolney, Green was carefully nursing himself, and made no impression on Holt, but both were leaving the Italians well behind At Bolney, Green was still two minutes behind Holt, who was feeling the effects of his effort Our man now began to cut down the lead and between Bolney and Pyecombe Holt had to take a rest. Green closed up on him and at Pyecombe had him well in sight Moving now in his fine style, Green passed Holt and started to walk away from him and opened up a gap which increased with each stride. The 'bus now went on to catch Green and cheer him on during the last stage of the race It now became evident that Green had an outside chance to break the long standing record of Ross Moral support was given to Green by the supporters, but it was of no avail, Green finishing 4 minutes outside the record, although putting up the second-best figures for this event. Green got a reception at Brighton that he can well be proud of. It was a great day for the Belgraves; not only providing the actual winner, they provided the winning team Green is a worthy champion of a champion club, and if he maintains his health and strength during the ensuing year, he is capable of beating the Brighton record next year and still adding further lustre to the walking lights of the Belgrave Harriers. It is very hard to convey in words the greatness of Green's walking, but in our next issue Mr J. B. Belchamber (and who is better qualified than "Jimmy" to write of the Brighton road and the races thereon?) will contribute an appreciation of Tommy's wonderful race and compare his times with those of the past giants. Our second man, Fred Rickards, walked surprisingly well, considering that but a few months before he had serious internal trouble which threatened stopping his walking career. Happily, he has made a good recovery and with Green and a newcomer, who did well at his first attempt and promises to do much better in the future, J. C. Bidgood, the Club become the first holders of the "Knott" Shield. Green, in addition to winning the "Victory" Cup, holds the "Belgrave" Cup for the Belgrave Long Distance Walking Championship, and Rickards and Bidgood gain Club medals for being second and third Club men home Of our other competitors, C A Wattam (who lives in Lincolnshire and makes an annual pilgrimage to London for the "Brighton") did well, as did Charlie Speechley and G. H. Laurie, another member we see but rarely. Stanley Manning did not do nearly so well as he has done in the past, but A. Martin and L. E. Fletcher are both to be congratulated on reaching Brighton safely—no mean feat (No joke intended). Previous to this year the following Club members had completed the journey inside nine hours :— E. G. Cooper, W. H. Hare, S. A. Manning and E. A Wall have finished inside 9hrs. 30min. The above figures show that we have a certain amount of tradition behind us in this race, and it was worthily upheld by our men this year. 1927—T. items.sum: Observer's column describing a typical club cross-country run, followed by short profiles of three members: J E. Tosh, N. R. Dewberry and B. J. T. Knifton.
items.s: SPORTS JOTTINGS Observer's column describing a typical club cross-country run, followed by short profiles of three members: J E. Tosh, N. R. Dewberry and B. J. T. Knifton. With the Cross Country Season just commenced I should like in the following article to give a brief idea of a cross country run. There was a decided nip in the air as I strolled along to our headquarters, but otherwise the weather was fine. On opening the door of the dressing room, a buzz of conversation greeted me Here were old acquaintances renewing their friendships, having perhaps not seen each other throughout the track season, but now all together again and looking forward to the afternoon's run A change into running attire, the packs are called out, slow, medium and fast, and we are off, jogging along over the country. My word, this is great, the keen air filling one's nostrils and banter being indulged in on all sides. A series of catcalls greet a runner who comes dashing into the lead and the pack leader gently admonishes him "Steady, boys, a hill here." Up and up. We are now at the top, breathing a little hard, perhaps, but on the flat once more we regain our breath and continue to go along at an even pace. " Ware ditch !" somebody shouts, and we all jump over in safety Here there is an obstacle to be climbed and then a stretch of down hill in which we take the opportunity of lengthening our stride and increasing speed. On the level again we have to steady a little as one or two are beginning to lag behind. "All up," comes the cry and we are off again, a jolly and contented crowd. Hereabouts there are a few anxious enquiries as to how much further before we reach home. "A mile,' appears to satisfy these questioners, mostly novices having their first experience of cross country running, and a few take heart from the knowledge that they are near home and begin to force the pace A word from the pack leader, however, curbs their spirit and we gradually draw nearer the end of our run. The starting field comes into sight and the pace quickens until with a few hundred yards to go, various little sprinting "dust-ups" are indulged in. On the road leading to the dressing room we all, however, form up again, and so we reach home. Here there is a quick flinging off of clothes, grabbing of towels, and a scamper off to be in the hot bath first. There is a babel of shouts, steam fills the air, and on all sides can be heard laughter and joking "Thwack !" somebody has caught a wet sponge in the ear There is a rush for the culprit and a scramble for the vacant place in the bath My word, how one's body glows when rubbing oneself down with the towel. You feel fit enough to jump over the moon. Slip on your outdoor garments, and then for a nice cup of hot tea and a piece of cake. "What's the time?" Oh, just right for my train at the station. A series of farewells and you depart convinced that there is no finer way of spending a Saturday afternoon than cross-country running. Football and hockey? Not in it, when compared with this sport, and you make a mental resolve to turn up at that away fixture next week and also to keep it up throughout the season. My next three Club members are as follows :— J E. Tosh, a fairly new member but one who soon shewed his paces by winning his first Club handicap, a success he followed by annexing his first Open one He then proceeded to win his next Club race, following which he won his next two Opens. Some going for a Junior, as he is yet in his teens Endowed with fine physique, he has immense possibilities and although his list of successes have been mostly over 880yds., it is yet early to say that this is his best distance Aspires to do cross-country running, but would do well not to overdo the serious side of it, using it as a medium for next track season. N. R. Dewberry, a member who has had a varied experience, having belonged to Slough and Surrey A.C. before joining us. Ran over the country last year, but was not then qualified for team events, so should be an asset to our teams this season. Has competed on the track with small success but will doubtless do better when he can find more time to devote to training. B. J. T. Knifton, a prominent member of our walking section and one of the younger members who promise to uphold our reputation as National Champions. Was a member of the winning team last year and should, with this experience, greatly improve in distance events. A good track walker, he met with success during the past season and also gained a first-class standard medal at the A.A.A.'s meeting. A very keen and live member and one who should continue to maintain the Club's high standard in walking. J. E. Tosh J E. Tosh fairly new member; won his first Club handicap and Open handicaps J E. items.s: THE ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING Report of the Annual General Meeting: membership and the season's successes, T. W. Green's 1929 walking record, the R. W. Best Cup to H. E Footer with his record, a presentation to W. J. Fish, the Treasurer's report, a rule change, and the officials elected. This year the Annual General Meeing was held at St. Gabriel's Hall, Lupus Street ("near the foot of Vauxhall Bridge !") and was fairly well attended. The Hon Secretary commenced his report by giving some details of the Club membership. He announced that 138 new members had joined during the past year, against 23 resignations, and said that the Club membership now stood at 508. In the matter of performances, the Club had just completed its best season yet, forty-two years after the formation of the Club. The walkers had opened the year by winning the R W A. scratch team cup and had finished by annexing the Brighton Walk Team Shield In between these two races, the National Championship had again been won (for the fourth time in five years) and second place gained in the Junior Championship held at Birmingham. The runners had also their share of wins. Both the Junior and Senior Championships of the South of the Thames Association had been won and also the Surrey Championship, by a very large margin. The Club's showing in the Southern and National Championships was disappointing after these early season wins, but amends were made in the London to Brighton Relay. In this race the Bels' finished seventh, gaining the special medals and completing the course in time which a few years ago would have beaten record. There had been two outstanding individuals during the past year, G. R. Dunckley and T W. Green. George Dunckley had represented England v. Germany in two races and had shown some remarkable running. He had been timed to do his stage of the 4 x 400yds. relay in 48 3-10 seconds—a wonderful performance. Tommy Green had shown notably consistent distance walking and the Club were justified in regarding him as the fastest man at the longer distances in the country, and possibly the world. His last performance, that of winning the Brighton walk in the second fastest time ever recorded, came as a fine finish to the year's efforts. His record follows :— In addition, he was first man home of our winning team in the National Championship, was the winner in the Hampshire 10 miles Championship, the Southern Railway Championship, and the English Railways v. French Railways (15 kilos) match, and holds Club Championships at three distances Truly, a remarkable season ! Green was then presented with the Club championship medal and in response to the general request for a speech, he said that he thought he was privileged to be able to help the Club in team races, and that he was always ready to do all in his power to help Belgrave. He modestly attributed the Club's win in the Brighton Team Race to Ferd Rickards who had only recently recovered from internal trouble, and J. C. Bidgood, the third man, who had done so well at the first attempt Mr. Bayliss then announced that the "R. W Best" Cup (awarded to the most successful competitor in Open events during the season) had been won by H. E Footer, and his further references to Boy Scout and Donjeroo meetings were drowned in laughter. Bert's record is a very imposing one and is as follows : A very pleasing presentation followed. Mr W J. Fish, a Vice-President and member of the Club for many years and our hard-working Clerk of the Course, was presented with a handsome clock as a mark of appreciation of his invaluable work during the past years. It is no easy task to prepare and mark out the track (often with no assistance) for the large fields we have had lately. Mr. Fish, in acknowledging the present, said that the Club could always rely upon him to do his utmost to make the Club meetings and functions successful. The Hon. Treasurer then gave his report He announced a profit on the past year of nearly £20, and pointed out that the Club's assets, as shown on the Balance Sheet, exceeded £500. A suggested alteration to the Club rules was passed, and provides that the number of Vice-Presidents that may be elected is unlimited (instead of being confined to sixteen as formerly), but that they shall not take part in the management of the Club unless otherwise elected to the Committee, and that the Committee should consist of ten members instead of eight as previously. The meeting then proceeded to elect officials for the coming year. Mr. W. H. Hare, in resigning his office of President, said that in his opinion the honour should go round, and he nominated Mr. E. Gordon, who was unanimously elected. W. L. Bayliss was re-elected as Hon Secretary, and E. A. Duffett and O. Horwood were also re-elected as Hon. Running and Walking Secretaries, respectively Mr H. Parker was elected Hon Treasurer in succession to Mr. A E Macher, who cannot now spare the time to discharge the duty, and W. A. Rice succeeds H L. Rollins as Hon. Social Secretary. Other officials were elected as follows :— Handicappers—J. B Belchamber (walking); L. E. Fletcher (running). Cross Country Captain—W. G. Webb. Vice-Captains—W A. Rice, T. J Flower. Track Captain—E. items.s: THE OPENING RUN. Report of the first Club handicap of the winter, a 3 mile road race round Wimbledon Common won by S. H. Warboys in a course record, with the results list (some printed handicap sums do not add up, e.g. A. E. Smith and A H Bulley; the text says 45 turned out, the results say 44 starters). The first Club handicap of the Winter Season was held on Saturday, October 5th This was the 3 Mile Road Race, run over the roads round Wimbledon Common A fine entry was received, namely 51, and 45 of these turned out, which promises well for the Club's strength during the coming season. G Tyrer, a veteran, who was second last year in the corresponding race, was limit man, and went off at his usual jog-trot. He was overhauled, however, after covering about a mile, Canard passing him in company with Colman and Strange S. H. Warboys was gradually closing the gap and at about the second mile he went into the lead, followed by Strange and Colman, with Canard losing ground. Jack Flower and A W Penny, the back-markers, were now coming through the field fast, but were still some way behind the leading trio. Coming into sight of home Warboys, who was leading by 40yds., lengthened out and eventually won easily in time which was wonderful, considering the conditions, for although the day was fine there was a tremendous head-on wind for the runners to battle against. His actual time, 14min. 55secs, beat the course record of 15min held by H. S Cook, which was also beaten this year by Jack Flower—another fine performance. C. R. Strange, in securing second place, ran well and pluckily in staving off a determined challenge by Colman, who was beaten into third place by 15yds. The latter has had a wonderful list of successes in recent Club handicaps; in fact it seems impossible to prevent him from securing a prize. He ran himself right out on Saturday, and as he is only just out of the Junior stage, he should do well in the forthcoming races, with careful training. F. G Ford (who was fourth, a position he has filled in several races during the past track season), finished with a fine sprint, but was just unable to catch the third man Still, he is a persevering runner and may break his unlucky run of fourth places ere long. Arthur Penny also ran well, keeping company with J. E. Flower, during the race and being a few yards behind him at the finish. The third member of the Flower family, A. J., nearly justified the high hopes of getting him placed, and ran really well; while Footer and Rice looked like making an impression on the field until troubled with the high wind. Our half-mile cracks, Scrimshaw and Tosh, both found the conditions a little too much for them, while Jack Williams, one of our most promising sprinters, found his dinner troubling him and promptly relieved himself of it! Of the 45 starters, 39 completed the course; quite a good average when one considers how early in the season it is for racing; coupled with conditions that were far from ideal. Which, of course, only serves to emphasise the greatness of Warboys' running, and we all look forward to him accomplishing some fine performances over the country RESULTS. items.sum: Report of the Club's opening 5 miles walking handicap, won by P N Khlopin from L. E Storey and Saunders, with the results (two printed actual times do not add up: W Dodkin 44 4 where 41 44 + 2 30 makes 44 14, and S. L King 46 59 where 43 25 + 3 35 makes 47 0).
items.s: THE OPENING WALK. Report of the Club's opening 5 miles walking handicap, won by P N Khlopin from L. E Storey and Saunders, with the results (two printed actual times do not add up: W Dodkin 44 4 where 41 44 + 2 30 makes 44 14, and S. L King 46 59 where 43 25 + 3 35 makes 47 0). This year 32 entries were received for the 5 miles handicap with which we usually open the season, and of these 27 started and 20 were timed in These figures are very encouraging, especially when it is remembered that about a third of those to finish the course were young walkers still in their 'teens and it seems that Belgrave prestige in walking circles will be as high in the future as it is now. Right from the start of the race it was evident that Paul Khlopin was almost unbeatable with 5min. 20sec. start, and at two miles he had taken the lead, which he never surrendered. Paul, who used to represent the Club in cross-country races, is now determined to do likewise at road walking, and he should prove an asset to our teams. His win was the reward for perseverance throughout the summer and he fully deserved his initial Club prize for walking. L. E Storey, one of the bright hopes of the future, walked well to gain second place and showed that he is equally at home on road or track Saunders, the third man, makes a habit of being placed in this race each year; for last year he was the winner, and in 1927 he was third. This is a good record and is evidence of continued improvement Of the others it must be said that both, in point of time taken and fairness of action they reached a high standard, as a glance at the table of results will show. Len Fletcher returned fastest time and Jack Rathbone second fastest—a good performance, for only three weeks before he was competing in the London—Brighton Race. H. C Larman proved to be the best of the newcomers, and he should lose his "novice" rank very soon. It is very pleasing to see S. L. King, a previous Walking Secretary, an active member once again, for his past performances (like those of our former President) were rapidly assuming a legendary character without a present-day basis of fact. To conclude, everything points to another successful season. There is the National Shield, the "Burman" Cup and the "Knott' Shield to be retained, and other honours to be won, including the "Junior" Championship. Is it our turn to win again this year? RESULTS. items.label: September 1929
items.h: THE LIGHTER SIDE OF THE CLUB LIFE
items.sum: Social notes by the Hon. Social Secretary on the Club's first social evening of the season at Wimbledon, its cabaret, and the coming Opening Dance at Wandsworth Town Hall.
items.s: THE LIGHTER SIDE OF THE CLUB LIFE Social notes by the Hon. Social Secretary on the Club's first social evening of the season at Wimbledon, its cabaret, and the coming Opening Dance at Wandsworth Town Hall. Our first Social of the season at Wimbledon on October 5th, was a great success both numerically and financially—not that finance is our first thought, but, naturally, it is very encouraging to find these affairs finish up on the right side It is the social success that is the main objective. Perhaps the idea of arranging it after the Road Races, using them as an added attraction, was the reason, but the fact remains that about 120 sat down to tea, and this number, I think, constitutes a record. There were a good number of London Olympiades amongst us, to whom, of course, we must tender our thanks But otherwise, it was purely a Club affair. We hold our next social evening on November 23rd, and I see no reason why even this figure should not be topped, as we shall have the support of visiting Clubs in St. George's Services S.C., Croydon H., Mitcham A.C. and Epsom H. It was very pleasing to see a number of track men present, for the Road Walking and Cross-Country Season is so long that it is only at these affairs that we can keep in personal touch with our fast men. The Club Magazine, of course, keeps them well versed with Club news, but we prefer to see them if only to find out the amount of fat they are putting on, or to give the officials an opportunity of collecting any subs. or such like that may be due! Reverting to our last Social, we tried a new Dance Band and it was generally voted a success. Billy Williams was in splendid form and he gets a better reception each time he appears. Charlie Boud also got over with a few songs and patter. One item (his own composition, I understand) should touch the Handicapper's heart, but we shall have to wait until Boxing Day to see, as Charlie doesn't race over the country. I think several members were agreeably surprised to see these two boys so ably accompanied by Len Fletcher on the piano. Charlie Strange then introduced his young sister, who showed us a few eccentric dance steps, and this effort concluded the cabaret part of the Social. I think among our membership now there must be some more talent in this direction. Boud and Williams, with one or two exceptions, have usually shouldered the whole programme, so I hope to hear of some applicants for inclusion in our second effort, on November 23rd Attention must now be drawn to the Opening Dance of the Season. This is to be held at Wandsworth Town Hall on Friday, November 1st, and if similar support is accorded this, as to the corresponding Dance of last year at this Hall, then there can be no doubt as to its success and judging by our first Social, I think it will be advisable to make early application for tickets, which will be 1/6 each as usual and are obtainable from — W. A. RICE, Hon Social Secretary, 36 Ascalow Road, S.W.8. items.label: September 1929
items.sum: Letter from Vice-President and former cross-country captain E Mussellbrook recalling the Club's lean pre-war years and its team placings in the 1913 and 1915 South of the Thames Junior Championships.
e: South of the Thames Junior Championship
items.s: CORRESPONDENCE Letter from Vice-President and former cross-country captain E Mussellbrook recalling the Club's lean pre-war years and its team placings in the 1913 and 1915 South of the Thames Junior Championships. (The following letter has been received from Mr. E Mussellbrook, a Vice-President of the Club and a former cross-country captain, and should prove of interest to all, whether "old-timers" or newcomers). Dear Mr. Editor, It is very pleasing to me as a member of some of the Belgrave pre-war cross-country teams, and as one who still retains his keenness, to read of the Club's successes and to notice the splendid team spirit which exists. This was particularly in evidence in the recent Jockey Cup Race. My running dates back to 1906, when I used to run for the now defunct Kennington Harriers. The "Bels." catered for boxing as well as athletics in those days and in 1912 I joined, together with many of the Club's stalwarts, Messrs. H Parker Oscar Horwood, H. Brown, etc, from the late Westminster Harriers. The years that followed were very lean ones and Oscar Horwood, being Secretary, often had to buy the prizes out of his own pocket, owing to lack of funds. The number of members could almost be counted on the fingers, but they were 100 per cent. Club men. The same few runners had to represent the Club both in Championships and Inter Club races. George Still at that time, was only a second-claim member and was running at his best, gaining some of the highest honours that are to be obtained at the cross-country game. We used to follow him over Richmond Park for speed work! They were strenuous times, but from the point view of comradeship, very happy ones, and, in my opinion, laid the foundation of our present Club Under the secretaryship of O. Horwood( then a runner) and Clem Arnold, the Club grew rapidly and, but for the War, would have come into prominence at a much earlier date. I give here two examples of our team packing, years ago — 1913—South of the Thames Junior Championship at Weybridge Winners, Weybridge A.C., 33pts.; Belgrave H. 3rd, 66pts. H. Parker 15th (32m. 4s.), O Horwood 16th (32m 7s); R W. Best 17th (32m. 8s); and E. Mussellbrook 18th (32m. 9s.). 1915—South of the Thames Junior Championship at Esher. Winners, Ashcombe A C., 20pts, Belgrave H 3rd., 61pts. E. Mussellbrook 13th (48m. 12s.), G. C. Arnold 15th (48m. 24s), J. Offen 16th (48m 29s.); and H. J. Sexton 17th (48m. 33s.). These were the only two championships in which we were placed during my running days with the Club, although the Bels had been placed in the Senior South of the Thames Race years before. The team spirit was the main thing, however, in those days, and if the Club continues with this ideal in view, all things will become possible, even the winning of the "National," or the Brighton Relay. Believe me, Yours truly, E MUSSELLBROOK. E. Surrey Youths' 3 mile cross country race
items.s: FORTHCOMING EVENTS Notice of coming fixtures: the Hon. Running Secretary's cross-country runs, training, rail fares and Surrey Youths' team call, followed by walking dates with enquiries to O. Horwood. On October 19th we have the first of the Inter-Club races between Ashcombe A.C, Thames Valley H., and ourselves. These are held over 5 mile courses and in this series of races the all-to-score rule operates, so that everyone competing has an interest in the race, by scoring for his club. This time the race is at Hounslow, from Thames Valley Harriers' new headquarters there, and we hope to see a good muster for our lads present. The 26th sees us journeying to Mitcham A C's abode at Rose Hill Farm, for a social run with Croydon H., Epsom H, and the home club. Following the run will be a social evening and we trust our members will support this, as you are always sure of a good time at Mitcham A C.'s headquarters On November 2nd we shall have the usual training runs from Wimbledon. Several packs will go out and we welcome any new members who would like to come along and have an amble over our country. All members who are qualified for the South of the Thames Junior race, to be held at Epsom on November 16th, should now be in strict training for this event. We entered four teams last year and we shall enter as many teams as possible this year. A team consists of 8 to run and 4 to score. In case the word Junior misleads some of our members, let me hasten to say that there is no age limit; it simply means that men who have been successful in previous years or in Senior races are barred. We won this race last year and are hoping that with the help of a new team we shall again be victorious. Cheap rail tickets can be obtained from either Section Secretaries or Mr. W. J. Fish. Clapham Junction to Wimbledon, return fare 6d.; Vauxhall to Wimbledon, return fare 8d. Our training quarters at the Rising Sun, Ebury Bridge Road, are now open on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and we hope our members will avail themselves of this opportunity for mid-week training. Runs start at 7-45 p.m. I should be pleased if any Junior members, under 18 years of age on day of race, with a Surrey County qualification and who intend to run over the country, will get in touch with me, with a view to selecting the team to compete in the Surrey Youths' 3 mile cross country race on December 7th. All enquiries to E. A. DUFFETT, Hon Running Sec., 138 Frant Road, Thornton Heath. Walkers should note the following dates .— Oct. 26—R W.A. Open Race. Nov. 9—Enfield A.C. Open Race. Our Open Walk will take place on November 30th, and on December 7th we are promoting a 5 miles Open Novice Walk. Any enquiries should be addressed to O. HORWOOD, 13 Abbott Avenue, Wimbledon, S W.20. items.label: July 1925
items.sum: Foreword to the second issue reporting a good reception but a modest response, and asking for volunteer distributors so the gazette can go monthly.
items.s: FOREWORD. Foreword to the second issue reporting a good reception but a modest response, and asking for volunteer distributors so the gazette can go monthly. FOREWORD. In making our second appearance we are pleased to state that our previous issue was quite well received and from the general tone of many communications to hand it certainly appears that “The Belgravian” has served a good purpose in keeping in touch and sustaining the interest of several members who might otherwise have dropped out of the Club and its activities. On the other hand we must candidly admit that the numerical response for support has not so far exceeded expectations. We are by no means dismayed or undaunted however, for we are only urged on to greater efforts to make our Gazette a better and greater success generally. We have never been afraid of a good deal of spade work to ensure any success. The record of the Club shows that very well as exemplified by our National Road Walking successes after years of hard work and disappointments. Gradual but sustained improvement will always outstay the meteoric success and “flash in the pan” achievements. It is all a matter of team work, and team work is probably just as much, or even more, desirable and necessary in Club work as it is in racing. Since we are anxious to be enabled to publish “The Belgravian” monthly, instead of quarterly as at present, we would be pleased to receive the names of any members who are in close touch with others, to act as distributors, in order to facilitate despatch and reduce postage expenses. We can then reconsider the whole matter of costing, but must again impress the fact that we want every member to subscribe to carry us through. Here is your opportunity for a little team work. Our request in the last issue for constructive criticism did not fail to receive the attention it deserved and some of the suggestions have been adopted as far as possible. Any further suggestions or matter for publication will be gladly received.

items.label: July 1925
items.sum: Letter from the President, R. W. Ricketts, congratulating members on the season, crediting the officers for the club's rise and urging the nearly 400 members to train hard.
items.s: CORRESPONDENCE RECEIVED. Letter from the President, R. W. Ricketts, congratulating members on the season, crediting the officers for the club's rise and urging the nearly 400 members to train hard. CORRESPONDENCE RECEIVED. To the Editor, Sir, I am very sorry that I was not able to write this letter in time for our last publication. Owing to a very busy Season I am not able to put in so much time as I should like with you, but I would add there is very little that happens without I know in some way or other. I must congratulate the members on their activities since we began the new Season. I have been asked by prominent members of other Clubs, how we account for our leap to fame. My answer was, that it is the officers of the Club who leave no stone unturned for the care and comfort of the members. It is with pride and admiration I look upon the Club which in turn will be as strong in running as it is in walking. And I look forward to every one of our, close approaching, 400 members to train hard to reach the top of their ambitions. Work hard for the Club and support our Social events. I wish now to take this opportunity to thank the Officers and members for the splendid help they have given in making the Club such a great success. Yours Sincerely, R. W. Ricketts, President. R. W. Ricketts R. W. Ricketts President
